c: Claude Code Ecosystem — Complete Guide ☰ Menu ← Back to Hub 🛠️ Claude Code Ecosystem 1. Foundation 2. Analogy 3. Journey 4. Conversations 5. Integration 6. Ripple Effects 7. Evolution 8. Patterns 9. Tradeoffs 10. Scale 11. Landscape 12. Pitfalls 13. Debugging 14. Eloquent 15. Practice 16. Reference 17. Ecosystem 18. Next Foundation & Context Claude Code is not a smarter autocomplete — it is a programmable AI operating system that reads your entire codebase, executes real shell commands, delegates to specialist sub-agents, and persists what it learns across sessions, all within a finite context window you must learn to manage like a scarce resource. Before you can use Claude Code fluently, you need a mental map of every moving part. This section builds that map — from first principles to the full layered architecture. The Full Architecture — One Diagram Every component of Claude Code exists in a deliberate layer. Understanding which layer something belongs to tells you how it behaves, how it loads, and what it can influence. USER INTERFACE LAYER ORCHESTRATION LAYER TOOLS LAYER EXTENSIONS LAYER PERSISTENCE LAYER VERSION CONTROL LAYER User Terminal CLI prompt — where you type instructions Main Agent (Director) Reads prompt, plans steps, calls tools, delegates sub-agents Explore Sub-Agent codebase search, file analysis Plan Sub-Agent architecture, task decomposition [own context window] [own context window] Bash Read / Write Edit Glob / Grep WebSearch Task (sub-agent) Skills & Plugins procedural knowledge, slash cmds MCP Servers GitHub, DBs, APIs — external tools Hooks shell cmds at lifecycle events IDE Integration VS Code, JetBrains side panels CLAUDE.md global + project + rules/ Auto Memory MEMORY.md — Claude writes for itself Settings .claude/settings.json Context Window ~200K tokens — finite, managed Git Worktrees parallel isolated agent sessions Branches one branch per worktree/agent Agent Teams peer-to-peer, shared task list The Claude Code architecture stack — six distinct layers, each with a clear responsibility. Data flows downward; results propagate back upward. Why Claude Code Exists — The Problem It Solves Before agentic coding tools, AI assistance in software development came in two forms: chat completions (ask a question, get a text answer, manually apply it) and autocomplete (Copilot-style, line-by-line suggestions). Both had a fundamental limitation: the AI could not act. It could only suggest. The Pre-Agentic Gap A developer working with GPT-4 or early Copilot had to mentally translate AI output into actions: copy the code, paste it into the file, run the tests, read the error, describe the error back to the AI, copy the fix. Every loop required a human to act as the bridge between AI insight and codebase reality. For simple tasks this was tolerable. For complex multi-file refactors, it was nearly unusable. The Agentic Shift Claude Code closes that gap. The AI is given direct tools: it reads files without being told their contents, executes shell commands and reads output, edits files directly, searches the codebase semantically. A single prompt like "add pagination to the users endpoint and update all tests" becomes a multi-step autonomous operation — not a suggestion, but an execution. The New Complexity With agency comes new cognitive load for the developer. You are no longer reviewing suggestions; you are directing an autonomous system. Context window management, sub-agent delegation, and memory persistence become skills you must actively develop. This is why the architecture matters — you cannot use what you cannot model. Historical Context — Three Generations of AI Coding 2020–22 Generation 1: Chat Completions GPT-3, early ChatGPT. Developers paste code into a web chat, ask questions, copy answers back. Zero integration with the IDE or terminal. The AI has no memory between sessions and no knowledge of the codebase beyond what you paste in. Useful for snippets; impractical for real development flows. 2021–24 Generation 2: Inline Autocomplete (Copilot Era) GitHub Copilot, Tabnine, Codeium. AI embedded in the IDE suggests completions as you type. Context is limited to the current file and a few open tabs. Fast and frictionless for boilerplate but fundamentally reactive — the AI waits for you to type. It does not plan, search, or execute. The human remains the agent. 2024 Generation 2.5: IDE-Integrated Agents (Cursor, Cody) Cursor, Cody, Windsurf. AI can now read multiple files and make multi-file edits. Still primarily IDE-native. The agentic capabilities exist but are constrained by the GUI paradigm. Great for individual developers but difficult to compose into larger automated workflows. 2024–25 Generation 3: Terminal Agentic Systems (Claude Code) Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI. AI lives in the terminal, not the IDE. It has full access to the filesystem, shell, and external APIs. It can spawn sub-agents, maintain persistent memory, load skills, and coordinate parallel worktrees. The developer becomes a director, not a typist. This is the current frontier. 2025+ Generation 4 (Emerging): Agent Teams and Multi-Repo Coordination TeammateTool (Opus 4.6, Feb 2026). Multiple peer agents collaborating in shared task spaces, messaging each other directly, operating across repositories simultaneously. The boundary between "one AI with tools" and "an organization of AIs" begins to dissolve. Claude Code is the current inflection point into this generation. Essential Abbreviations These terms appear throughout every conversation about Claude Code. Knowing them cold — not just their expansions but their architectural roles — is the mark of someone who has spent real time in the system. CLI Command Line Interface What it means: You interact with Claude Code by typing commands into a terminal window, not by clicking buttons in a GUI. This is intentional — terminal access means full system access. In practice: You run claude in your project directory. Everything from there is text in, text out — including Claude reading files, running tests, and reporting results. SDK Software Development Kit What it means: The Agent SDK is the underlying framework that powers Claude Code's agentic capabilities — tool calling, sub-agent spawning, context management. Claude Code is built on top of it. In practice: When a sub-agent is described in system prompt documentation as "powered by the Agent SDK," it means that sub-agent can call tools, spawn its own child agents, and has its own isolated context window. MCP Model Context Protocol What it means: An open standard (created by Anthropic) for connecting AI models to external tools, data sources, and APIs. MCP servers are lightweight processes that expose tools Claude can call — think of them as adapters between Claude and the outside world. In practice: A GitHub MCP server lets Claude list issues, create PRs, and merge branches. A Postgres MCP server lets Claude query your database directly. Configured in .claude/settings.json . LLM Large Language Model What it means: The AI model itself — Claude Sonnet, Claude Opus, etc. The LLM is the "brain" of the agent. Everything else (tools, memory, context) is infrastructure built around the LLM to give it the ability to act in the world. In practice: When people say "the model hallucinated," they mean the LLM generated plausible-sounding but incorrect output. When you choose between Sonnet and Opus, you are choosing which LLM the agent runs on — with different capability and cost trade-offs. CLAUDE.md The Project Memory File What it means: A markdown file that Claude reads at the start of every session. It contains standing instructions, project context, coding standards, and anything else Claude should always know. It is the closest thing to a "system prompt you can edit." In practice: A well-crafted CLAUDE.md might include: which test framework the project uses, which files are off-limits, how commit messages should be formatted, and the company's API rate limits. It lives in version control and is shared with the whole team. SKILL.md The Skill Definition File What it means: A markdown file with YAML frontmatter that defines a skill — a reusable, named procedure Claude can discover and execute. Skills are to Claude Code what npm packages are to Node: installable, shareable units of capability. In practice: A "deploy to staging" skill contains the steps Claude should follow when asked to deploy. A "generate migration" skill knows how to create database migration files following your project's conventions. Discovered and loaded automatically when relevant. API Application Programming Interface What it means: A defined contract for how software components communicate. In the Claude Code context, the Anthropic API is what Claude Code calls to get completions from the model. MCP servers expose their own APIs that Claude calls via the MCP protocol. In practice: Every prompt you type in Claude Code results in one or more API calls to Anthropic. Each call consumes tokens (and therefore money). Context window management is, at its core, API cost management. What This Foundation Unlocks With this architecture in your mental model, every other concept in this learning journey will click into place. When you hear "context compaction," you will know which layer is being compressed and why. When you hear "MCP server with lazy loading," you will know which layer is being optimized and what the performance trade-off is. Architecture first — everything else follows. Living Analogy — The Film Production Studio Every piece of the Claude Code ecosystem maps perfectly to a film production role — and once you see the studio, you can never un-see it. Good analogies are not decorative. They are cognitive scaffolding. This one will let you explain any Claude Code concept to any engineer — even one who has never used it — by grounding it in a world everyone already understands. Start Simple: The Director and the Script Every film starts with two things: a director and a script. The director is a creative problem-solver who reads the script, forms a vision, and then marshals every resource of the studio to bring that vision to life. The script is the specific, bounded request — not a vague wish, but a concrete creative brief. The Director The director does not write the code. The director does not write the tests. The director does not check the server logs or look up the API docs. The director delegates all of that — but holds the vision and makes the final call on every decision. Critically: the director is responsible for the result even though specialists do the work. "I delegated it" is never an excuse for a bad film. The Main Agent The main agent receives your prompt and forms a plan. It reads files to understand the codebase, breaks the work into steps, decides which steps need specialist delegation, and assembles the final result. The main agent is responsible for what Claude does. If it misunderstands the intent or delegates poorly, the output will be wrong — regardless of how well the sub-agents performed their individual tasks. The Script A script is not a finished film. It is a precise description of what should happen, in what order, with what intent. A vague script ("make something exciting") produces chaos. A good script leaves room for interpretation but is unambiguous about outcomes. Your Prompt Your prompt is the script. Vague prompts produce unpredictable results. Specific prompts — "refactor the authentication module to use JWT, maintain backwards compatibility with existing sessions, update all tests" — give the agent a clear brief with defined success criteria. The Production Bible — Standing Rules for Every Crew Member Every major film production maintains a Production Bible: a master document that defines the visual style, the tone, the character rules, the world-building constraints. Every department — costume, set design, visual effects, sound — reads the bible before beginning work. It ensures coherence across a production involving hundreds of people over years. CLAUDE.md is the Production Bible CLAUDE.md is loaded into context at the start of every Claude Code session. Every sub-agent Claude spawns also loads relevant CLAUDE.md files. It contains the rules that are always true: the testing framework, the commit message format, the files that should never be modified, the company's infrastructure constraints, the performance budgets. Without a Production Bible, every crew member makes their own style decisions. The result is inconsistency. Without a well-crafted CLAUDE.md, Claude will make its own decisions about coding conventions, test structure, and documentation style — and those decisions may not match your team's standards. The Hierarchy: Global, Project, and Rules Folders A studio might have company-wide standards (the studio's house style) and project-specific overrides (this film's unique requirements). Claude Code has the same hierarchy: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (global, applies to every project), ./CLAUDE.md (project-level, versioned in git and shared with the team), and .claude/rules/ (modular rules files, introduced in v2.0, for domain-specific standing instructions). Each layer narrows and refines the one above it. Department Heads — Sub-Agents with Their Own Call Sheets A film director does not personally operate every camera, mix every audio track, and design every costume. They hire department heads — experts in their specific domains — and give each department head a call sheet that defines what they need to accomplish today, with what resources, and by when. Main Agent Director — holds the vision Explore Agent Cinematographer Searches codebase, finds relevant files, maps dependencies own context window Plan Agent Production Designer Architecture decisions, task decomposition, change planning own context window Bash Agent Key Grip Runs commands, executes tests, checks server output own context window Custom Agent Specialist (your spec) Domain-specific work, custom system prompt, restricted tool access own context window delegates tasks with call sheets (task description + tool permissions) sub-agents return results to parent context Each sub-agent is a department head with its own context window — isolated from the main agent, focused on its domain, reporting back when done. Why Context Isolation Matters A cinematographer does not need to know every line of dialogue, every costume decision, or every music cue. They need to know their shots. Sub-agents work the same way: each one loads only what it needs into its own context window. This means the main agent's context window is not burdened by the full details of every sub-task — only by the results. The main agent stays focused on direction; the sub-agents handle the details. Equipment Rental Houses — MCP Servers A production does not own every piece of equipment it needs. For a crane shot, you rent a crane. For underwater filming, you rent an underwater housing rig. The rental house has the specialized equipment; you bring it on set only for the scenes that need it. MCP Servers are Equipment Rental Houses A GitHub MCP server is a crane: you bring it in when you need to reach high (create PRs, manage issues, browse repository structure). A Postgres MCP server is an underwater rig: specialized, powerful, and only needed for specific scenes (querying production data, generating migration scripts). You configure which rental houses (MCP servers) are available in .claude/settings.json — but you only pay the setup cost once, and Claude loads them lazily when the specific capability is needed, saving ~95% of context token overhead. Shooting Scripts — Skills A shooting script is more detailed than the main script. It specifies camera angles, lighting setups, actor positioning, and the exact sequence of events for each scene. The cinematographer uses it as a step-by-step recipe that has been proven to produce a specific visual result. Skills are Shooting Scripts A skill is a named, procedural set of instructions for a specific type of task. A "deploy-to-staging" skill contains the exact sequence of steps Claude should follow — check branch status, run tests, build Docker image, push to registry, update Kubernetes config, verify health checks. It is not a suggestion; it is a proven procedure. Skills live in folders with a SKILL.md file, are discovered automatically when Claude determines they are relevant, and can be shared across projects and teams through the skills.sh marketplace (20,000+ skills available as of Feb 2026). Skills vs MCP: A Critical Distinction Skills are procedural knowledge (how to do something). MCP servers are external connectivity (access to something). A skill might say "to deploy, follow these steps." An MCP server gives Claude the tools those steps require. You need both — but they solve different problems. Confusing them leads to over-engineering one and under-investing in the other. The Dailies Room — Auto Memory After each day of filming, the director and department heads review "dailies" — the raw footage from the day. Important notes get written into a shared log: "the lighting in scene 14 skewed warm, compensate in post," "Actor A ad-libbed a line that works better than the script, use it in continuity." These notes inform tomorrow's shooting without requiring everyone to rewatch every day's footage. Auto Memory is the Dailies Log Claude writes notes to ~/.claude/projects/[project]/memory/MEMORY.md automatically during sessions. When it discovers something important about your codebase — a tricky dependency, a performance constraint, an undocumented API quirk — it writes a note so future sessions do not need to rediscover it. The first 200 lines of MEMORY.md load into context automatically at session start. This is not human-authored documentation; it is AI-authored institutional knowledge, growing organically as Claude works in your project. Film Stock — The Context Window In the era of physical film, a cinematographer had a finite number of reels. Every shot consumed film stock. The editor had to work within the total stock available to produce a coherent film. Excessive coverage — filming every angle of every scene "just in case" — burned through stock and often left the editor with too much unusable material. The Context Window is Your Film Stock Budget Claude's context window is approximately 200,000 tokens. Every file read, every shell command output, every sub-agent result, every tool call response consumes tokens. When the budget runs low, quality degrades — Claude begins to lose track of earlier context. Like a film editor working with limited stock, you must make active decisions about what to keep in context and what to cut. This is not a bug; it is the fundamental constraint of the medium, and mastering it is the difference between a coherent production and an incoherent one. The Editing Bay — Context Compaction A three-month shoot might produce 600 hours of raw footage. The final film is 2 hours. The editor's job is not to discard the shoot — it is to distill it. The essential story is preserved; the redundant coverage, the failed takes, and the lengthy setup shots are cut. The result tells the same story in a fraction of the space. Compaction is the Editing Bay The /compact command (or auto-compaction when the context nears capacity) summarizes the conversation history, replacing verbose earlier exchanges with a distilled summary that preserves decisions, context, and intent without token-for-token replay. You can guide the editor: /compact focus on the authentication refactor we started tells Claude what story to preserve. The "Compact Instructions" section in CLAUDE.md gives standing direction to the auto-compaction process — the equivalent of a director giving the editor notes before they cut. Second-Unit Directors — Git Worktrees Large productions run second units: a smaller crew that shoots background plates, location establishing shots, and action sequences simultaneously with the main unit. The second unit director works independently from the main director, on a different location, producing footage that will be integrated in editing. Both units film simultaneously; neither waits for the other. Git Worktrees are Second Units Git worktrees create separate filesystem directories, each pointing to a different branch of your repository. You can run Claude Code sessions in each worktree simultaneously — one Claude fixing a bug on a hotfix branch while another implements a new feature on a feature branch. They share the git repository but have completely independent working directories. When you use the "worktree" keyword in a sub-agent definition, that sub-agent gets its own isolated worktree — preventing one agent's changes from interfering with another's during parallel execution. The Full Studio Lot — Agent Teams A film studio lot does not produce one film at a time. Multiple productions run simultaneously: different stages, different directors, different crews. But the studio infrastructure — props warehouse, costume department, back lot — is shared. Directors can call each other, coordinate shoot schedules, and share resources. They are independent but aware of each other. Agent Teams are Multiple Productions on the Studio Lot Agent Teams (experimental, powered by TeammateTool in Opus 4.6) allow multiple Claude sessions to run as peers rather than in a parent-child hierarchy. Unlike sub-agents (which only talk to their parent), teammates can message each other directly. They share a task list for coordination. One teammate might be handling the backend refactor while another handles the frontend changes and a third writes documentation — all in parallel, all aware of each other's progress through the shared task list. This is not a simple feature addition; it is a different model of how AI-assisted development can work at scale. The Full Analogy Map at a Glance Director - Main Agent Script - Your Prompt Production Bible - CLAUDE.md Department Heads - Sub-Agents Equipment Rentals - MCP Servers Shooting Scripts - Skills Dailies Notes - Auto Memory Film Stock - Context Window Editing Bay - Compaction Second Unit - Git Worktrees Studio Lot - Agent Teams Call Sheet - Task / Tool Permissions Learning Journey — Four Levels Claude Code mastery is not a single leap — it is four distinct gear shifts, each requiring you to unlearn the caution of the previous level and build a new kind of confidence. Most people plateau at Level 2 because the jump to Level 3 requires thinking about the system, not just using it. This map will show you exactly where you are and what the next gear shift demands. Where Are You Right Now? 1 Don't Break It Week 1 — Month 3 2 Comfortable Practitioner Month 3 — Year 1 3 Problem Solver Year 1 — Year 2 4 Architect's Mind Year 2+ Level 1: Don't Break It Level 2: Practitioner Level 3: Problem Solver Level 4: Architect Level 1: "Don't Break It" Week 1 through Month 3 — Production Assistant on Set The Film Analogy: You Are the Production Assistant You have just arrived on set. Your job is not to direct. Your job is to watch how things work, not get in the way, learn the etiquette, and deliver messages accurately. You are surrounded by professionals who are better at their jobs than you are at yours. Humility and observation are your primary assets at this stage. The worst mistake a production assistant makes is overconfidence — assuming they understand the full production before they have observed enough sessions to know what they do not know. What This Level Looks Like You have installed Claude Code. You are giving it simple, bounded tasks: "read this file and explain what it does," "write a unit test for this function," "fix this linting error." You are reviewing every change before accepting it. You feel nervous when Claude proposes to modify more than a few files. That nervousness is healthy. Core Survival Checklist /help — Run this immediately. Read the full output. Know what commands exist before you need them urgently. /clear — Know how to wipe conversational context without losing your CLAUDE.md. This is your emergency reset when Claude gets confused about the session. /compact — Understand that this summarizes context and reduces token usage. Use it proactively on long sessions, not just when things feel slow. Review every file change — Claude shows you a diff. Read it. Every time. You are responsible for what lands in your codebase. Use git before asking Claude to do anything risky — Commit your current work. If Claude makes a mess, you want a clean rollback point. Read the CLAUDE.md documentation — Understand what Claude.md is, where it lives, and that creating a good one is your first real leverage point. Observe context window usage — Run /context to see how much of the window is in use. Develop an intuition for how fast it fills. Start with small, reversible tasks — "Add a docstring to this function." Not "refactor the entire authentication system." Build trust incrementally. Level 1 Success Signals You can give Claude a bounded task and get a useful result at least 70% of the time without needing to re-prompt You never accept a change without reviewing the diff You know the difference between /compact, /clear, and /context You have written at least a minimal CLAUDE.md for one project You have experienced at least one "Claude got confused" session and recovered from it cleanly The Most Common Level 1 Mistake Giving Claude too much scope too early, then blaming Claude when the result is wrong. "Rewrite all our API endpoints to use async/await" is not a Level 1 task. It is barely a Level 3 task without strong guardrails. Scope creep in prompts is the #1 cause of Level 1 frustration. Start so small it feels trivial. What to Read While at This Level The official Claude Code documentation (docs.anthropic.com/claude-code). Focus on: CLAUDE.md reference, tool descriptions, slash command list, and the context window management guide. These are your Production Assistant's crew handbook. Level 2: "Comfortable Practitioner" Month 3 through Year 1 — Department Head Running Your Own Crew The Film Analogy: You Are Now a Department Head You have been on enough productions to know how a set works. You have your own crew — junior developers who follow your lead, a codebase you understand well, and a set of tools you reach for instinctively. You can direct your department without asking the director how to frame a shot. You make independent decisions within your domain and deliver results the director can build on. What This Level Looks Like You have crafted a meaningful CLAUDE.md for your primary project. You use skills from the marketplace. You have connected at least one MCP server (probably GitHub). You are comfortable letting Claude handle multi-file changes after a quick plan review. You have started experimenting with sub-agents for specific tasks. You think about context budget before starting long sessions. Key Capabilities to Develop CLAUDE.md Craft Move beyond a minimal CLAUDE.md to a curated one. Include: tech stack with versions, test commands, lint commands, deployment procedures, off-limits files, coding conventions, the team's preferred naming patterns, and any infrastructure constraints. Think of it as the onboarding doc you wish you had when you joined the team — written for an AI that reads it before every session. Film analogy: your Production Bible is now a real bible — detailed, authoritative, version-controlled. Junior department heads can now work from it without your supervision. Sub-Agent Usage Use sub-agents for tasks that require deep, isolated focus: "explore the codebase and find all places where this error pattern could occur" is a good Explore sub-agent task. "Plan the database schema changes required for this feature" is a good Plan sub-agent task. The key insight: sub-agents preserve the main agent's context budget for high-level decision-making. Film analogy: you now delegate whole departments instead of individual tasks. Your call sheets are clear, your expectations are concrete, and you review results rather than doing the work yourself. Skills Installation and Use Browse skills.sh and install skills relevant to your stack. A "generate-migration" skill for your ORM. A "deploy-to-staging" skill for your CI/CD pipeline. A "create-component" skill for your frontend framework. Once installed, Claude discovers and uses them automatically when you describe a relevant task. You do not need to invoke them by name. Film analogy: you now have shooting scripts for standard shot types. You do not reinvent the over-the-shoulder dialogue setup every time — you follow the proven procedure. MCP Server Configuration Configure at least a GitHub MCP server and your primary database MCP server. Understand that MCP servers are lazy-loaded — they do not consume context until Claude needs a tool from them. Understand that each MCP server exposes a set of tools (functions Claude can call), not just data. Film analogy: you have established relationships with the key equipment rental houses for your production type. You know what each house carries, and you can get the gear quickly when a scene needs it. Level 2 Success Signals Your CLAUDE.md meaningfully improves Claude's output quality on the first attempt for project-specific tasks You have at least 3 skills installed and Claude uses them without you naming them You can delegate a multi-file refactor to a sub-agent and review the result You proactively run /compact before context-heavy operations, not just when forced to You have connected at least one MCP server and verified Claude uses it effectively The Most Common Level 2 Plateau Using Claude as a faster way to do the same things you did before. Real Level 2 requires changing your workflows, not just adding Claude to old ones. If you are still manually writing migration files after every schema change, you have not fully internalized Level 2. Systematically identify your most repetitive 5-minute tasks and build skills or CLAUDE.md instructions that automate them. Level 3: "Problem Solver" Year 1 through Year 2 — The Line Producer Optimizing the Whole Production The Film Analogy: You Are the Line Producer The line producer does not direct creatively. They optimize the entire production: budget, schedule, crew efficiency, equipment logistics. They see the whole machine and make it run faster and cheaper without compromising the director's vision. They are the production's operational brain. At Level 3, you think about Claude Code as a system to be optimized, not just a tool to be used. What This Level Looks Like You are actively managing context window strategy for complex, multi-hour sessions. You are using git worktrees to run parallel Claude sessions on separate branches. You have written custom skills for your team's specific workflows. You understand why a session drifted and how to prevent it. You can debug unexpected Claude behavior systematically rather than just re-prompting and hoping. Advanced Capabilities This Level Demands Advanced Context Window Management At Level 3, you do not just react to context pressure — you architect against it. This means: using sub-agents aggressively to keep the main agent's context focused on high-level orchestration, pre-loading only the files Claude will need (not the whole repo), setting "Compact Instructions" in CLAUDE.md to guide auto-compaction, and knowing when to start a fresh session vs. compacting the current one. Film analogy: you are now tracking film stock consumption per scene, per day. You know exactly when the budget will run out and you are planning reshoots before you need them. Git Worktree Workflows Running parallel Claude sessions in worktrees is one of the highest-leverage techniques at Level 3. One session works on a feature branch while another handles a bug fix, and a third runs the full test suite. You coordinate via git — each session commits to its own branch; you review and merge when complete. The ccpm pattern (using GitHub Issues as a task queue for worktree-based parallel execution) is worth studying at this level. Film analogy: you are now coordinating second, third, and fourth units simultaneously. Each has its own director, its own schedule, and its own deliverables — but you are ensuring they do not step on each other's feet. Custom Skills Authoring You are no longer just installing skills from marketplaces — you are writing them. A skill for your company's specific deployment pipeline. A skill for your database migration conventions. A skill for generating API documentation in your house style. The SKILL.md format is simple (YAML frontmatter + markdown instructions), and the leverage is enormous: one well-written skill saves every developer on your team the same effort every time it runs. Film analogy: you are now writing your own shooting scripts for shots that do not exist in the standard manual. Your production has unique requirements; your procedures reflect that. Hook-Driven Automation Hooks run shell commands at specific lifecycle events: session start, tool calls, config changes. At Level 3, you use hooks for: injecting dynamic context at session start (current branch name, recently modified files, active GitHub issues), running safety checks before certain tool calls, and triggering notifications when long-running sub-agents complete. Film analogy: you have automated the production infrastructure. The slate board is updated automatically before each take. The crew is notified automatically when the lighting setup is ready. Human error is removed from the repeatable parts of production. Debugging Agent Behavior When Claude behaves unexpectedly, a Level 3 practitioner diagnoses root cause rather than re-prompting blindly. Common root causes: context pollution (earlier in the session, incorrect information was loaded and is influencing current decisions), CLAUDE.md ambiguity (conflicting instructions), tool permission mismatch (a sub-agent was given access to tools that conflict with the task), and context compaction loss (the compaction summary lost a critical decision that was made earlier). Film analogy: you are now the person who can watch dailies and immediately identify whether a problem came from camera, lighting, performance, or post-production. You have seen enough productions to diagnose by symptoms. Level 3 Success Signals You can maintain a productive Claude Code session for 4+ hours on a complex feature without context degradation You run parallel worktree sessions routinely for independent workstreams You have written and deployed at least 3 custom skills that your team uses regularly When a Claude session produces unexpected output, you can identify the root cause within 5 minutes You use hooks for at least one automated workflow The Level 3 Trap Over-engineering the Claude Code setup to the point where maintaining it consumes more time than the productivity gains justify. CLAUDE.md becomes a 500-line specification document. Skills multiply until nobody knows what is installed. Hooks become a hidden dependency that breaks inexplicably when the infrastructure changes. Level 3 requires judgment about when to add complexity and when to keep it simple. The goal is leveraged productivity, not a showcase of Claude Code mastery. Level 4: "Architect's Mind" Year 2+ — Studio Head Greenlighting Productions The Film Analogy: You Are the Studio Head The studio head does not direct films. They greenlight them. They set the strategy for which productions the studio should invest in, build the infrastructure that all productions share, hire the directors, and create the organizational culture that makes consistently great films possible. At Level 4, you are no longer just using Claude Code — you are deciding how your organization uses it, building the shared infrastructure, and defining what "good" looks like for your context. What This Level Looks Like You are designing Claude Code rollouts for teams of 20, 50, or 500 developers. You are building custom plugins that bundle skills, MCP servers, and hooks into deployable packages. You are thinking about multi-repo coordination, enterprise security requirements, and how to measure whether AI-assisted development is actually producing better software faster. You mentor others and can explain why the ecosystem works the way it does, not just how to use it. Architect-Level Capabilities Agent Team Orchestration Agent Teams (experimental, Opus 4.6, enabled via CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS) allow Claude sessions to act as peers: direct peer-to-peer messaging, shared task lists, independent context windows. Level 4 requires understanding when this model outperforms sub-agent hierarchies and when it introduces coordination overhead that degrades performance. The architectural question is: is the work decomposable into genuinely independent streams, or does the coordination cost exceed the parallelism gain? Film analogy: you are now deciding when to run multiple simultaneous productions and when to focus all resources on a single flagship film. The infrastructure exists for both models; the wisdom is in choosing. Enterprise Rollout Patterns Deploying Claude Code to 50 developers requires addressing: shared CLAUDE.md in version control (which conventions are universal, which are team-specific), a curated skills library distributed via a private skills registry, MCP server configurations deployed via infrastructure-as-code, security hooks that enforce compliance requirements (no pushing to main without review, no accessing production databases without audit logging), and training paths calibrated to each level of this journey. Film analogy: you are building the studio infrastructure that all productions share — the back lot, the equipment inventory, the safety protocols — so that individual directors can focus on their films without reinventing the wheel. Custom Plugin Development Plugins bundle slash commands, agents, MCP servers, and hooks into a deployable unit. A Level 4 practitioner builds plugins for their organization's needs: a "onboarding" plugin that equips every new Claude session with the team's standards, a "security-audit" plugin that runs compliance checks, a "release" plugin that orchestrates the full deployment pipeline. With 9,000+ public plugins available and the plugin install mechanism at /plugin, the ecosystem is dense — but custom plugins for proprietary workflows are where the real leverage lies. Film analogy: you are not just using the studio's equipment — you are commissioning specialized gear built specifically for your production style. You are contributing back to the craft. Multi-Repo Coordination Large systems span multiple repositories. A backend service, a mobile app, a shared library, an infrastructure repo. Changes to the shared library require coordinated updates across all consumers. At Level 4, you design Claude Code workflows that span repositories: a coordinating agent that understands the dependency graph and orchestrates changes across repos in the correct order, with proper isolation and rollback capability at each step. Film analogy: you are now coordinating a cinematic universe — multiple directors, multiple franchises, all needing to maintain narrative coherence across productions that run for years. Mentoring and Culture Building Level 4 is incomplete without the ability to bring others to Level 2 and 3 effectively. This means: designing onboarding experiences that accelerate the Level 1 learning curve, articulating the mental models clearly enough that developers who have never used Claude Code can start using it correctly from day one, and creating organizational norms around AI-assisted development that preserve code quality and engineering judgment rather than trading them for velocity. Film analogy: you are now running the studio's director development program. Your job is not to direct films yourself — it is to develop directors who make films better than you could. Level 4 Success Signals You have designed and deployed a Claude Code setup for a team of 10+ developers with measurable productivity improvements You have built at least one custom plugin that others depend on You can articulate when Agent Teams are the right choice vs. sub-agent hierarchies, with concrete criteria Developers you have mentored have independently reached Level 2 within their first month You think about Claude Code's architectural constraints as design inputs, not limitations to work around The Level 4 Question That Does Not Have a Good Answer Yet As of February 2026, nobody has fully solved the problem of measuring the quality impact of AI-assisted development at scale. Velocity increases are easy to measure (story points, PRs merged, bugs fixed). Whether the codebase is more maintainable, better tested, and more coherent in its architecture after a year of heavy AI-assisted development — that is a harder question. Level 4 practitioners are actively grappling with this, and the honest answer is: we do not know yet. Build your measurement frameworks now; you will need them when your organization's leadership asks. Cross-Level Principles That Never Change The Principle That Holds at Every Level At every level of Claude Code mastery, the developer is responsible for the output. Claude is a powerful collaborator, not an autonomous replacement for engineering judgment. The difference between Level 1 and Level 4 is not "how much you trust Claude" — it is "how precisely you direct Claude." More experienced practitioners write more precise prompts, build better guardrails, and design better feedback loops. Their Claude sessions produce better results not because Claude is smarter, but because they are better directors. Avoid the "AI Did It" Attribution At every level, code that lands in your codebase is your code — regardless of who wrote the first draft. "The AI made that architectural decision" is not a defense a principal engineer can use. Review everything. Understand everything you merge. The goal of Claude Code is to make you more productive, not to replace your engineering judgment with AI judgment. Protect that judgment jealously. Interview Conversations The questions below are not trivia tests — they are invitations to demonstrate architectural thinking. A weak answer lists features. A strong answer explains tradeoffs, constraints, and design rationale. Seven questions, each with talking points, follow-up traps, and a production story that grounds the abstract in lived experience. Study these until you can answer each one without looking. Q1. What is Claude Code and how does it differ from GitHub Copilot? Architecture Core Talking Points Paradigm difference, not feature difference. Copilot is reactive autocomplete — it waits for you to type and suggests continuations. Claude Code is an agentic system — it receives a goal, plans a sequence of actions, executes them using real tools, reads results, and iterates until the goal is achieved. The human's role shifts from typist to director. Execution vs. suggestion. Copilot produces text suggestions that you accept or reject. Claude Code reads actual files from your filesystem, runs real shell commands, modifies real files, and reads test output. It operates in your environment, not in a sandbox that approximates it. Context scope. Copilot's effective context is the current file plus a few open tabs — call it a few hundred to a few thousand tokens in practice. Claude Code has a ~200K token context window and can actively search the codebase using Glob, Grep, and Read tools to load exactly what it needs. It understands the whole system, not just the current screen. Tool and extension ecosystem. Copilot is IDE-native and UI-bound. Claude Code has a first-class extensibility model: Skills (procedural knowledge), MCP Servers (external connectivity), Plugins (bundled capabilities), and Hooks (lifecycle automation). Each adds capabilities that Copilot's architecture cannot accommodate. Memory and persistence. Copilot has no memory across sessions. Claude Code has CLAUDE.md (loaded every session), auto memory (written by Claude, read at session start), and project-level context that accumulates over time. Follow-Up Questions to Expect "Is Claude Code always better than Copilot?" — No. For low-context completion tasks (finishing a for loop, completing a method signature), inline autocomplete is faster and less disruptive. Claude Code shines on multi-step, multi-file, goal-oriented work. They are different tools for different jobs. "What are the risks of giving an AI direct shell access?" — This is a good follow-up. The answer involves the importance of CLAUDE.md guardrails, pre-commit hooks, the developer's responsibility to review every action, and why the terminal context (where the developer is already operating as a privileged user) is the right place for this kind of tool. "How does context window size affect the comparison?" — Larger context means Claude can hold more of the codebase in mind simultaneously. But it also means more tokens per session, which means more cost. Context management strategy is what separates effective Claude Code users from expensive ones. Production Story The authentication migration scenario: A team needed to migrate from session-based auth to JWT across a Rails monolith — 47 files involved. With Copilot, this would take a senior engineer 2-3 days: manually finding all auth touchpoints, writing each change, running tests, fixing failures. With Claude Code, the engineer wrote a detailed prompt describing the migration requirements, Claude used Grep and Glob to map every auth touchpoint, proposed a migration plan, executed changes file-by-file while running the test suite after each batch, and completed the initial migration in 6 hours. The engineer spent that time reviewing diffs and handling the 4 edge cases Claude flagged it could not resolve confidently. The result was not "Claude did it" — it was "the engineer directed a tireless senior developer." Q2. Explain the CLAUDE.md memory hierarchy. Memory Core Talking Points Four distinct tiers, four distinct purposes. Global CLAUDE.md (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) applies to all projects — personal preferences, global tool configurations, universal coding style. Project CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md) applies to the specific project, lives in git, and is shared with the team. Rules folder (.claude/rules/) introduced in v2.0 (January 2026) allows domain-specific modular rules — one file for testing conventions, one for deployment, one for security requirements. Auto memory (~/.claude/projects/[project]/memory/MEMORY.md) is written by Claude itself during sessions — not human-authored, but Claude-authored institutional knowledge. Loading order and precedence. At session start, Claude loads CLAUDE.md files in order: global, then project, then relevant rules. More specific files can refine or override more general ones. The first 200 lines of MEMORY.md are also loaded automatically. This happens before you type your first prompt — it is the pre-production briefing before the shoot begins. Auto-compaction interaction. The "Compact Instructions" section of CLAUDE.md guides what the auto-compaction algorithm preserves when it summarizes conversation history. This is the mechanism by which your standing instructions shape how Claude manages its own context window — meta-programming the production's editing workflow. MEMORY.md vs. CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md is human-authored and static between sessions (unless you edit it). MEMORY.md is AI-authored and grows dynamically — Claude writes to it when it discovers important context: a tricky dependency, an undocumented behavior, a performance constraint. The first 200 lines load automatically; everything beyond requires explicit reference. Managing MEMORY.md quality is a Level 3 concern: periodically reviewing, pruning irrelevant notes, and structuring it so the most important information lands in the first 200 lines. Team sharing implications. Project CLAUDE.md belongs in version control. It is the team's shared set of AI-facing conventions — as important as your linting configuration or your CI pipeline. Treat it as a first-class engineering artifact: review it in PRs, update it when conventions change, onboard new team members through it. Follow-Up Questions to Expect "What happens if CLAUDE.md files conflict?" — More specific files take precedence. Project overrides global; rules override both. If genuine conflicts exist, Claude will flag them. This is why global CLAUDE.md should be abstract (style preferences) and project CLAUDE.md should be concrete (project-specific commands). "How do you prevent CLAUDE.md from becoming a dumping ground?" — Structure it deliberately: a short summary at the top (the 30-second brief), then sections for development environment, testing, deployment, conventions, and off-limits areas. Ruthlessly prune instructions that Claude follows correctly without being told — only document the non-obvious. "How does this compare to cursor rules or system prompts?" — Conceptually similar but architecturally richer: the hierarchy (global/project/rules/memory), the auto-compaction instruction capability, and the auto memory system are unique to Claude Code's model. Production Story The MEMORY.md gold mine: A senior engineer at a fintech startup noticed after three months of daily Claude Code use that MEMORY.md had grown to 800 lines. On review, they found Claude had documented: the fact that the payment processing service was on an older API version that rejected certain content-type headers, a race condition in the test suite that would fail non-deterministically when run in parallel, the specific Postgres configuration that caused query plan changes on certain dataset sizes, and 14 other quirks discovered during sessions. This was institutional knowledge that existed nowhere else in the codebase. The engineer promoted the most critical 20 items to CLAUDE.md and shared them with the team as a "Claude's discoveries" doc. The auto memory system had been building an undocumented project knowledge base the whole time. Q3. How do sub-agents work and when would you use them? Orchestration Core Talking Points Context isolation is the primary benefit. Sub-agents run in their own context windows, completely isolated from the main agent. This means a sub-agent can load an entire module's codebase, analyze it deeply, and return a result — without that analysis consuming the main agent's context budget. The main agent stays focused on orchestration; sub-agents handle depth. Parallel execution is the performance benefit. Multiple sub-agents can run simultaneously. In worktree isolation mode, each sub-agent operates in its own branch with no filesystem contention. Three sub-agents analyzing three independent components in parallel compress a 3-hour analysis into a 40-minute one. Delegation patterns. Good sub-agent tasks are bounded, well-defined, and returnable: "find all places in the codebase where we use this deprecated API," "generate a comprehensive test suite for this module," "analyze the performance characteristics of these three query patterns." Bad sub-agent tasks are vague, open-ended, or require continuous main-agent judgment: "improve the codebase" is not a sub-agent task. Custom system prompts and tool permissions. Sub-agents can be given custom system prompts (making them specialists in a domain) and restricted tool access (a sub-agent that only analyzes code should not have Bash access to execute it). This principle of least privilege improves both safety and focus. The "worktree" keyword. Adding "worktree" to a sub-agent's configuration gives it an isolated git worktree to work in. Changes it makes do not affect the main branch until explicitly merged. Critical for sub-agents that modify files — prevents interference between parallel agents and gives you a clean review boundary. Follow-Up Questions to Expect "How does the main agent know when to delegate vs. do the work itself?" — This is a judgment call that improves with experience. A useful heuristic: if the task requires reading more than ~20% of your context budget in files, or if it is genuinely independent of other work in progress, it is a candidate for sub-agent delegation. "What is the cost model for sub-agents?" — Each sub-agent is a separate context window, which means separate token consumption and (with API-based models) separate billing. Many sub-agents on long tasks can multiply cost. The trade-off is context preservation in the main agent vs. total token spend. "How is this different from Agent Teams?" — Sub-agents are parent-child: the main agent spawns them, they report back. Agent Teams are peer-to-peer: teammates can message each other directly and share a task list. Sub-agents are generally more appropriate for well-defined delegation; Agent Teams are more appropriate for genuinely collaborative work where agents need to coordinate in real time. Production Story The parallel codebase audit: A team needed to audit their 300KLOC Node.js monorepo for three classes of issues: insecure direct object references, missing input validation, and SQL injection vectors. Sequentially, this would take days. Instead, the engineer defined three sub-agents, each assigned one class of issue, each with read-only tool access (no modifications), each running in parallel. All three ran simultaneously for 45 minutes. The main agent received three structured reports and synthesized them into a prioritized remediation plan. Total time: 90 minutes, of which the engineer was actively involved for perhaps 20. The context window strategy was elegant: each sub-agent loaded only the code relevant to its issue class, none of them burdened the main agent with 300KLOC of source, and the main agent's context was fully available for synthesis and planning. Q4. What are skills, and how do they differ from MCP servers and plugins? Extensibility Core Talking Points Skills = procedural knowledge. A skill is a named, reusable procedure — a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter that describes a workflow Claude should follow for a specific type of task. "How do I deploy to staging?" is a skill. "How do I generate a database migration for our ORM?" is a skill. Skills encode the how — the step-by-step process that, without the skill, Claude would either invent from first principles or ask you about repeatedly. MCP Servers = external connectivity. An MCP server is a lightweight process that exposes tools Claude can call to interact with external systems: GitHub (create PRs, list issues), databases (run queries), cloud providers (deploy services), internal APIs (fetch data). MCP servers do not contain procedures; they provide capabilities. The procedure for how to use those capabilities might live in a skill. Plugins = bundled collections. A plugin is a deployable package that bundles slash commands, agents, MCP servers, and hooks into a single installable unit. If a skill is a shooting script and an MCP server is an equipment rental relationship, a plugin is a complete production package — everything a new production team needs to start filming a specific genre of film. Installed via /plugin; 9,000+ available as of February 2026. The interplay. A deploy plugin might contain: a "deploy-to-staging" skill (the procedure), a cloud provider MCP server (the connectivity), a pre-deploy hook (safety check), and a /deploy slash command (the entry point). All four work together; none is a substitute for another. The Agent Skills open standard. Skills use a cross-platform open standard — a SKILL.md in the same format works in Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, Cursor, and Gemini CLI. Skills built for one platform are portable. The skills.sh marketplace has 20,000+ skills; skillsmp.com and skillhub.club provide alternative registries. This portability is a significant ecosystem advantage over proprietary extension formats. Follow-Up Questions to Expect "When would you choose a skill over just writing a detailed prompt?" — A skill encodes proven procedure. If you find yourself writing the same detailed prompt more than twice for a specific type of task, it is a candidate for a skill. Skills also benefit the whole team automatically once shared — a detailed prompt helps only the person who remembered to write it. "How are custom slash commands related to skills?" — Since v2.0 of Claude Code, custom slash commands and skills are the same underlying mechanism. A slash command is just a skill with a specific invocation trigger. The unification simplified the mental model significantly. "What is the lazy loading benefit for MCP servers?" — By default, Claude loads tool descriptions from all configured MCP servers at session start, consuming context budget. Lazy loading via MCP Tool Search loads tool descriptions only when Claude determines they are needed for the current task — reducing context overhead by approximately 95% for sessions that do not use all configured servers. Critical for teams with many MCP servers configured. Production Story The migration workflow composition: A platform team at a SaaS company needed every developer to follow a specific database migration procedure: generate the migration, validate backward compatibility, test the migration against a snapshot of production data, run the test suite, and create a PR with a standardized description format. Before skills, this was a 6-page runbook that half the team had not read. After: one skill (migration.md) encoding the complete procedure, one MCP server (internal database tools), one hook (loading current schema into context at session start). A developer types "create a migration to add indexes to the users table" and Claude follows the full procedure automatically. The runbook became executable. Q5. Walk me through context window management in Claude Code. Context Management Core Talking Points The context window is a finite resource — treat it like one. Claude's effective context window is approximately 200,000 tokens. Every file read, shell command output, sub-agent result, and conversational turn consumes tokens. As the window fills, two things happen: performance degrades (older context is effectively down-weighted) and costs rise (more tokens per request). Proactive management is not optional at Level 3+. /context for visibility. The /context command renders a visual representation of context usage: a colored grid showing what is consuming tokens, with a categorical breakdown (conversation history, file contents, tool results). Running /context at the start of a complex session establishes your baseline; running it periodically shows you the burn rate. Developers who never run /context are flying blind. /compact for controlled reduction. /compact summarizes the conversation history, replacing verbose earlier exchanges with a distilled summary. You can guide it: "/compact focus on the authentication refactor, discard the early exploration" tells Claude what story to preserve. The "Compact Instructions" section in CLAUDE.md provides standing guidance for the auto-compaction algorithm — the most powerful lever for teams that want consistent compaction behavior. /clear for a clean slate. /clear wipes all conversational context but CLAUDE.md and auto memory survive. Use it when a session has become so polluted or confused that compaction cannot recover it. The cost: you lose all session context. The benefit: you start fresh with only the standing knowledge that actually belongs to the project. Auto-compaction and its triggers. Auto-compaction fires automatically when the context window approaches capacity. If you have not set Compact Instructions in CLAUDE.md, the algorithm makes its own choices about what to preserve.
