Whats Next Section 01 · Foundation Foundation & Context Docker is a process isolation system that packages an application and all its dependencies into a portable, self-contained unit — solving the "works on my machine" problem by making the machine part of the artifact. The One-Sentence Truth Docker doesn't virtualize hardware. It isolates processes using Linux kernel primitives — namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource control — and wraps a layered filesystem around them so you can ship that isolated environment as a single artifact. Why Docker Exists — First Principles Before Docker, deploying software meant one of two things: either you installed it directly on the host (dependency hell) or you spun up a full Virtual Machine (slow, heavy, wasteful). The gap between development and production was enormous. The problem had two axes. First, dependency isolation : App A needs Python 3.8, App B needs Python 3.11, and the OS can only have one. Second, environment parity : the developer laptop has different libraries, kernel patches, and config than the production server. Docker solved both by making the environment a first-class artifact that travels with the code. The key insight was using existing Linux kernel features that had existed since 2008 (namespaces) and 2007 (cgroups) — Docker didn't invent new technology, it made existing technology accessible and composable. The Architecture Diagram Docker Architecture — Host OS to Container Physical Hardware (CPU · Memory · Disk · Network) Host OS Kernel (Linux) namespaces cgroups UnionFS / OverlayFS Docker Daemon (dockerd) API Server · Image Builder · Network Manager · Volume Manager · containerd shim Container A App Code Runtime/Libs Container B App Code Runtime/Libs Container C App Code Runtime/Libs Image Layers Layer 3: App (R/W) Layer 2: Deps (R/O) Layer 1: Base OS (R/O) Docker CLI docker build / run / push Registry Docker Hub / ECR / GCR REST API pull/push The Linux Kernel Primitives 🏠 Namespaces Isolate what a process sees . Each container gets its own PID space, network interfaces, filesystem mounts, hostname, user IDs, and IPC. The process thinks it's alone on the machine. 🎛️ cgroups (Control Groups) Limit what a process can use . CPU shares, memory limits, I/O bandwidth, network priority. Without cgroups, one container could starve all others. 📚 OverlayFS / UnionFS Stack read-only image layers and add a thin writable layer on top. 20 containers can share the same 500MB base image while each has its own 1MB write layer — massive disk savings. 🔒 seccomp + Capabilities Restrict which syscalls a container process can make and drop dangerous Linux capabilities (like CAP_NET_ADMIN). Defense in depth for container security. Key Concepts & Abbreviations Image vs Container ▼ Image = a read-only, layered blueprint. Like a class in OOP. It's a filesystem snapshot plus metadata (what command to run, what port to expose). You can't run an image directly — it's a template. Container = a running instance of an image. Like an object instantiated from a class. Docker adds a thin writable layer on top of the image layers, starts the specified process in an isolated namespace. Kill the container, the writable layer is gone (unless you have a volume). Dockerfile ▼ A recipe for building an image. Each instruction ( FROM , RUN , COPY , CMD ) creates a new immutable layer. Layers are cached by their content hash — if nothing changed, Docker reuses the cached layer. This is why order matters: put rarely changing instructions first (OS packages) and frequently changing ones last (app code). Registry ▼ A server that stores and distributes Docker images. Docker Hub is the public default. ECR (AWS Elastic Container Registry), GCR (Google Container Registry), ACR (Azure Container Registry), and Harbor are common private options. Images are referenced as registry/repo:tag — e.g., docker.io/nginx:1.25-alpine . Docker Compose ▼ A tool for defining and running multi-container applications using a YAML file. Instead of running three docker commands manually (start postgres, start redis, start app), you define all services, networks, and volumes in one docker-compose.yml and run docker compose up . Essential for local dev. Often replaced by Kubernetes in production. Docker Daemon (dockerd) ▼ The background service that does the actual work — managing containers, images, networks, and volumes. The Docker CLI communicates with it via a REST API over a Unix socket ( /var/run/docker.sock ). Since Docker 1.11, dockerd delegates container lifecycle to containerd , which delegates low-level operations to runc (the OCI runtime). This decoupling allowed Kubernetes to adopt containerd directly, bypassing Docker entirely. Volume vs Bind Mount vs tmpfs ▼ Volume : Docker-managed persistent storage at /var/lib/docker/volumes/ . Survives container restarts and removal. Best for databases, persistent data. Docker handles backups and migrations. Bind Mount : Mounts a specific host directory into the container. Your local ./src mounted at /app/src — changes on either side reflect immediately. Great for development, dangerous in production (host path dependency). tmpfs : In-memory only, never written to disk. Use for sensitive data like secrets that shouldn't persist, or for speed with ephemeral caches. The OCI Standard Open Container Initiative In 2015, Docker, CoreOS, and others formed the OCI to standardize container formats and runtimes. This was critical: it meant Kubernetes could run containers without requiring Docker at all. OCI defines: Image Spec (how images are structured and stored), Runtime Spec (what a container runtime must do), and Distribution Spec (how images are pushed/pulled). Any OCI-compliant tool can build, ship, and run containers interchangeably. Historical Context 2008–2012 The Pre-Docker World Linux containers (LXC) existed but required deep kernel expertise. Puppet/Chef managed VM configuration. Heroku pioneered "buildpacks" for app packaging. The problem was understood; the solution was painful. 2013 Docker 0.1 — dotCloud's Internal Tool Goes Public Solomon Hykes demos Docker at PyCon. Initial release wraps LXC with a simple CLI and layered images. The shipping container metaphor immediately resonates with developers. 2014–2015 Ecosystem Explosion Docker Compose (formerly Fig), Docker Swarm, Docker Machine. Every cloud provider adds container support. Mesosphere, CoreOS, and Kubernetes enter the orchestration space. Docker ships its own runtime (libcontainer, replacing LXC). 2016–2017 The Orchestration Wars Docker Swarm vs Kubernetes vs Mesos. Kubernetes, backed by Google's production experience with Borg, gradually wins. Docker Inc. eventually bundles Kubernetes alongside Swarm. 2019–2022 Kubernetes Deprecates Docker Kubernetes removes dockershim in v1.24. This doesn't mean containers go away — it means containerd (the runtime Docker uses internally) becomes the direct interface. Docker images still work fine. 2023–Present Maturity & Specialization Docker Desktop remains the dominant developer experience. Podman gains traction for daemonless, rootless containers. BuildKit becomes the default builder. Container security (Sigstore, SLSA) becomes priority. WASM containers emerge as a new frontier. ← Overview Living Analogy → Section 02 · Analogy The Shipping Container Revolution In 1956, Malcolm McLean invented the standardized shipping container. Before that, moving goods between ships, trains, and trucks was a labor-intensive nightmare of custom crates and re-packing. Docker did the same thing for software. 🚢 Shipping Containers : Global Trade = Docker Containers : Software Deployment Before standard shipping containers, moving cargo between ship, train, and truck required custom handling at every interface. Before Docker, deploying software between dev, staging, and prod required custom configuration at every environment. Layer by Layer: Building the Analogy Layer 1 — The Simple Version A shipping container is a standardized steel box . It doesn't care if it contains electronics, bananas, or machine parts. The port, ship, train, and truck don't care either — they all work with the same standard dimensions and coupling mechanisms. A Docker container is a standardized software box . It doesn't care if it contains a Python web server, a Node.js API, or a Java microservice. The CI server, cloud provider, and developer laptop don't care either — they all work with the same OCI-standard format. Layer 2 — Images Are the Blueprints Before filling a container, you have a manifest — a document describing exactly what goes inside and how it should be arranged. You can copy this manifest and fill 1,000 identical containers. A Docker image is this manifest-plus-contents. The Dockerfile is the specification for building that image. Once built, you can instantiate thousands of identical containers from a single image. The image itself never changes — containers are its instances. Layer 3 — Layers Are Intermodal Standardization Shipping containers standardized the interface — the corner castings, dimensions, and locking mechanisms. Inside, goods can be arranged however needed. The standardized interface (OCI) is what allows any crane (Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, containerd) to lift any container. Docker's image layers work similarly. Every image layer is a content-addressed blob. Layer 3 (your app code) sits on top of Layer 2 (Node.js runtime) which sits on top of Layer 1 (Alpine Linux). Ten different apps can share that Alpine layer — one copy on disk, referenced by all. Like containers sharing a chassis design while carrying different cargo. Layer 4 — The Registry Is the Shipping Depot In global shipping, goods flow through container depots — warehouses where containers are stored, tracked, and dispatched. You push a container to the depot; a ship pulls it when needed. Docker Hub, ECR, and GCR are the depots. You docker push an image from your CI pipeline to the registry; your Kubernetes cluster pull s it when deploying. The registry stores, versions, and distributes images globally. Layer 5 — Orchestration Is the Shipping Company Maersk doesn't personally load every container. They operate a logistics system that decides: which ship, which port, which schedule, how to handle failures (a delayed ship doesn't cancel your order — they re-route). They manage hundreds of thousands of containers worldwide. Kubernetes is Maersk. It decides which node runs which container, how many replicas to run, what to do when a container dies, how to roll out new versions without downtime. Individual containers are interchangeable — Kubernetes manages the fleet. The Full Mapping Shipping World Docker World Why It Matters Shipping Container Docker Container Standardized, portable, self-contained unit that works everywhere Container Blueprint / Manifest Dockerfile + Image Reproducible recipe for the exact same container every time Container Depot / Port Container Registry Central store for pushing, versioning, and pulling images Ship / Train / Truck Host OS / Cloud VM The carrier doesn't care what's inside — only the interface matters ISO Standard (20ft/40ft) OCI Spec Interoperability across all vendors and tools Crane Container Runtime (runc) The thing that actually lifts/starts a container Shipping Company (Maersk) Kubernetes / Docker Swarm Orchestrates fleet of containers across multiple carriers Manifest of Cargo Container metadata / labels Describes what's inside without opening the container Refrigerated Container Container with resource limits Specialized environment constraints for specific cargo/workloads Same goods, different packages Same image, different containers Multiple running instances from one image template Where the Analogy Breaks Down Analogy Limits — Don't Over-Extend Containers share a kernel . Physical containers are fully isolated. Docker containers share the host OS kernel — a kernel vulnerability can affect all containers on that host. Shipping containers don't share a hull. (This is why Kata Containers and Firecracker exist for stronger isolation.) Containers can talk to each other . Containers on the same Docker network can communicate freely by service name. Physical containers in a depot don't have a private phone network between them. Containers are ephemeral by design . Shipping containers hold physical goods that must be preserved. Docker containers are disposable — the filesystem is thrown away when they stop. Data must be externalized to volumes. Startup is nearly instant . A container starts in milliseconds. Loading a physical shipping container takes hours. This speed fundamentally changes how you architect systems (short-lived batch jobs, function-as-a-service). Apply the Analogy as You Learn Throughout this learning journey, when you encounter a new Docker concept, ask yourself: "What's the shipping equivalent?" 🏷️ Image Tags → Container Versions Like product serial numbers. nginx:1.25-alpine is a specific container spec, not just "nginx". Always pin tags in production. 🔌 Port Mapping → Dock Connection A container's internal port 8080 is like an internal loading door. Port mapping (-p 80:8080) is connecting the external dock to that specific door. 🗄️ Volumes → Bonded Warehouse Goods (data) stored outside the container in a secure facility, retrieved when the next container arrives. The container is interchangeable; the data persists. 🌐 Docker Networks → Private Shipping Lanes Containers on the same network can find each other by name. Isolated from external traffic. Custom lanes between trusted partners. ← Foundation Learning Journey → Section 03A · Learning Journey Four Levels of Docker Mastery Docker mastery isn't about memorizing flags — it's about progressively understanding what problem each feature solves. Here's the journey from first container to fleet architect. 🌱 Level 1 — "Don't Break It" · 0–6 Months The Beginner Mindset At this stage, Docker feels magical and slightly scary. You can run containers but aren't sure what's happening underneath. The goal is to build a correct mental model without over-engineering. What you can do: Run official images from Docker Hub ( docker run nginx , docker run postgres ) Write basic Dockerfiles with FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, EXPOSE Map ports ( -p 8080:80 ) and understand why this is necessary Use docker ps , docker logs , docker exec -it for basic debugging Use Docker Compose for local multi-service development Understand images vs containers conceptually Common mistakes at this level: Running everything as root inside the container Putting secrets in Dockerfiles (they get baked into the image!) Using latest tag instead of pinned versions One giant RUN command that can't be cached, or too many tiny ones creating layer bloat Storing persistent data inside the container filesystem (loses on restart) Mental model to develop: Think of a container as a very lightweight VM — a self-contained process with its own filesystem, not a full OS. The Dockerfile is a recipe. The image is the baked cake. The container is a slice. Level 1 Exit Criteria You can containerize a simple web application, connect it to a database using Docker Compose, and explain to a colleague what an image vs container is. ⚙️ Level 2 — "Comfortable Practitioner" · 6 Months–2 Years Building Real Production Images You now understand the basics and are building real applications. The focus shifts to doing Docker well — smaller images, faster builds, proper networking, and security hygiene. What you can do: Multi-stage builds : Use a builder stage (with compilers and dev tools) and copy only the artifact into a minimal runtime image. Node.js app that was 1.2GB becomes 85MB. Layer caching strategy : Structure Dockerfiles so package manifests are copied and installed before source code — avoids reinstalling all dependencies on every code change. Non-root users : Create a dedicated user in the Dockerfile with specific UID/GID. Understand why running as root is dangerous (container escape → host root). Docker networking : Bridge networks, host networking, DNS resolution by service name. Know when to use each. .dockerignore : What not to send to the build context (node_modules, .git, .env files). Health checks : HEALTHCHECK instruction so orchestrators know when a container is truly ready. BuildKit : Enable DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 for parallel builds, better caching, secret mounts, SSH forwards. Key insights at this level: Image size matters more than you think . A 1GB image vs 50MB image means 950MB less to pull on every deploy across every node in your cluster. At 100 nodes, that's 95GB of unnecessary transfer. Layers are forever . If you add a secret in one RUN command and delete it in the next, it's still in the image's layer history. Use BuildKit secret mounts or multi-stage builds to keep secrets out of layers. The Multi-Stage Build Revelation The moment you write your first multi-stage build and watch a 1.4GB Go build image shrink to a 12MB scratch binary — that's the Level 2 breakthrough. The production image doesn't need compilers, test frameworks, or development headers. Compose skills to develop: Depends-on with health checks (not just service name ordering) Environment files and variable substitution Named volumes vs bind mounts for the right scenarios Compose override files for dev/test/staging environments Network isolation between service groups 🔧 Level 3 — "Problem Solver" · 2–5 Years Containerization Strategy & Operations You can now evaluate whether to containerize something and make architectural decisions about how. You've seen production incidents and know what breaks. You're thinking about the whole system, not individual containers. What you can do: Container security posture : Read-only root filesystems, seccomp profiles, AppArmor/SELinux profiles, capability dropping. Run docker scout or Trivy for vulnerability scanning in CI pipelines. Custom bridge networks with static IPs : For legacy applications that hardcode IP addresses (yes, they exist). Container resource constraints : CPU shares, memory limits, memory swap, CPU pinning. Know what OOMKilled means and how to tune limits without starving neighbors. Production logging strategy : JSON log driver, fluentd/Fluentbit sidecar, stdout to centralized logging. Why app logs shouldn't go to files inside containers. Private registry operations : Set up Harbor or ECR, configure image scanning, mirror policies, garbage collection, access controls. Build pipeline optimization : Registry-based caching in CI/CD, remote build contexts, build secrets management. Container patterns : Sidecar, Init containers, Ambassador, Adapter patterns (you think in patterns, not just individual containers). Key insight: Containers are not VMs Level 3 practitioners stop treating containers like lightweight VMs. A VM is a computer; a container is a process with a fancy filesystem . This changes everything: containers shouldn't run multiple services, shouldn't use a process supervisor like systemd, and shouldn't have SSH installed for debugging. Operational thinking: You think about image supply chain: who publishes the base image? Is it verified? Do you mirror base images to avoid Docker Hub rate limits pulling in CI? What's the CVE patching strategy when a critical vulnerability hits OpenSSL and your base image ships an old version? 🏛️ Level 4 — "Architect's Mind" · 5–15+ Years Container Platform Strategy At this level, you're making organizational decisions. You're deciding whether containers are the right tool, designing internal developer platforms (IDPs), setting organizational standards, and evaluating emerging runtimes. What you think about: Build vs Buy vs Adopt : Should teams build their own Dockerfiles? Adopt a golden base image? Use a builder platform (Buildpacks, ko for Go, Jib for Java) that abstracts Dockerfiles entirely? Image governance at scale : How does an organization with 200 microservices manage base image updates? Automated PRs? Shared base images with versioned releases? The dependency graph of base images. Container runtime selection : Docker vs containerd vs Podman vs CRI-O — what's the right choice for your Kubernetes cluster? Kata Containers for multi-tenant untrusted workloads? Build system integration : How Docker integrates with Bazel, Gradle, Maven, npm workspaces for monorepo builds. Remote caching. Hermetic builds for reproducibility. The next frontier : WASM containers (Spin, WasmEdge) for function-sized workloads. Firecracker microVMs for stronger isolation. Distribution-less images. The Architect's Central Question "Docker is a tool that solves the packaging and distribution problem. The harder problems — scheduling, service discovery, load balancing, health management — require an orchestrator. When should we use containers? When should we use serverless? When should we use PaaS? The answer changes based on team size, workload shape, and operational maturity." What an architect knows that others don't: The difference between a container runtime (runc), container engine (Docker), and container orchestrator (Kubernetes) — and why this layering matters Why Docker removed from Kubernetes didn't break anything (containerd was already doing the real work) The OCI spec is what enables the entire ecosystem — it's the most important thing Docker gave the industry Containers solved packaging; service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) solves the networking complexity that containers created Most "Docker problems" in production are actually Linux resource management, networking, or application design problems ← Analogy Interview Prep → Section 03B · Interview Interview Conversations 7 interview question trees — each with a strong opener, follow-up paths, production stories, and the nuanced answer that shows real-world experience. Click any question to expand. Interview Strategy Don't recite definitions. Start with the problem the feature solves, then explain the mechanism, then give a production example. Interviewers at senior levels want to hear "we ran into X, which taught us Y." 1. "Explain how Docker containers differ from Virtual Machines. Why would you choose one over the other?" ▼ Strong Opener "The fundamental difference is what gets virtualized . A VM virtualizes the hardware — you get a simulated CPU, memory, and disk, with a full guest OS kernel on top. A Docker container virtualizes only the process environment — it shares the host kernel but gets isolated namespaces and resource limits. This makes containers start in milliseconds instead of minutes and use megabytes instead of gigabytes." The Technical Depth "Docker achieves isolation through two Linux kernel mechanisms: namespaces (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user) give each container its own view of system resources, and cgroups enforce resource limits on CPU, memory, and I/O. There's no hypervisor, no guest OS — the container process runs directly on the host kernel." The Trade-off Nuance "But this kernel sharing is also the security boundary difference. With a VM, a compromised guest needs a hypervisor escape to reach the host. With containers, a kernel exploit in the shared kernel can affect all containers. For multi-tenant environments serving untrusted code — think public cloud workloads — VMs or microVMs like Firecracker are still the right choice." When to choose which Choose containers: fast iteration, microservices, consistent dev/prod environments, cost efficiency at scale Choose VMs: strong security isolation, different OS kernels required (Windows on Linux host), compliance requirements, untrusted workloads Choose both: Kubernetes nodes are VMs, but pods are containers — you get VM-level node isolation + container-level workload density Likely Follow-ups → "What if I need to run a Windows container on a Linux host?" (Docker Desktop does this via a hidden Linux VM) → "How does container density compare to VMs?" (10-100x more containers per host) → "What's Kata Containers?" (OCI-compatible containers backed by lightweight VMs) 2. "Walk me through how you'd build a production-ready Docker image for a Node.js application." ▼ Strong Opener "A production-ready image needs to be minimal, reproducible, secure, and cache-efficient. I'd use a multi-stage build : a full Node.js builder stage that installs all dependencies and runs the build, followed by a minimal runtime stage (Node Alpine) that only copies the production artifact. This can take a 1.5GB image to under 100MB." Layer Caching Strategy "The critical caching insight: copy package.json and package-lock.json first, run npm ci , then copy the rest of the source. Since package.json rarely changes, the dependency installation layer gets cached on 90%+ of builds. Without this ordering, every source code change triggers a full npm install." Security Hardening "I'd create a non-root user (node user already exists in the official Node image), use --chown when copying files, set USER node before the CMD, and use a read-only root filesystem where possible. I'd also run npm ci --only=production to exclude dev dependencies from the runtime image, and pin the Node version (not latest )." What I'd include / exclude Include: HEALTHCHECK with curl or wget, ENTRYPOINT for signal handling (or use tini ), explicit EXPOSE Exclude: npm, git, build tools, test files, .env files, .git directory (via .dockerignore) Secrets: never in ENV instructions or RUN commands — use BuildKit secret mounts or runtime secrets Production Story "At a previous job, we had a CI pipeline where every deployment took 8 minutes just to build the Docker image. After restructuring the Dockerfile to copy package files first and using BuildKit's registry cache, we got it to 45 seconds for unchanged dependencies. This unblocked the team from doing multiple daily deployments." Follow-ups → "How do you handle environment-specific config?" (Env vars at runtime, not build time) → "What about base image vulnerabilities?" (Automated scanning in CI, Dependabot for base images) → "Distroless images?" (No shell, package manager — smallest possible attack surface) 3. "How does Docker networking work? How do containers communicate with each other?" ▼ Strong Opener "Docker creates virtual networks using Linux bridges and veth (virtual Ethernet) pairs. Each container gets a network namespace with a virtual interface connected to a Docker bridge network. Containers on the same bridge network can communicate using service names — Docker's embedded DNS resolver maps service names to container IPs automatically." The Four Network Drivers bridge (default): Private virtual network on the host. Containers communicate by IP or service name. Traffic to the outside world is NAT'd through the host IP. host : Container uses the host's network namespace directly. No network isolation. Used for performance-critical applications or when you need to expose many ports. Dangerous in multi-tenant environments. none : No networking. Completely isolated. Useful for batch jobs that process files without any network. overlay : Multi-host networking for Docker Swarm. Uses VXLAN tunnels to span containers across multiple Docker hosts. Kubernetes uses a similar concept with CNI plugins (Flannel, Calico, Cilium). DNS Resolution "When you run docker-compose up, each service gets a DNS entry matching its service name. So your app can connect to postgres:5432 instead of an IP address. This is done by Docker's internal DNS server (127.0.0.11) injected into each container's /etc/resolv.conf ." Port Mapping Mechanics "Port mapping (-p 8080:80) creates an iptables rule that NATs traffic from host port 8080 to the container's internal port 80. The container process binds to 0.0.0.0:80 inside its network namespace; external traffic hits the host's 8080 and gets forwarded." Security Consideration "By default, containers can reach any other container on the same bridge network. For microservices, it's best practice to create separate user-defined bridge networks per service tier and explicitly connect containers that need to communicate. This prevents a compromised container from reaching unrelated services." 4. "What's the difference between Docker volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs? When do you use each?" ▼ Strong Opener "This is fundamentally about where data lives and who controls it . Volumes are managed by Docker and stored in Docker's data directory — portable, easy to back up, Docker controls the path. Bind mounts reference a specific host path — the host controls it, and any change on either side is immediately visible. tmpfs is ephemeral in-memory storage that never touches disk." When to use each Volumes for production database data, any persistent state in production. Docker manages them, they work across platforms, they're the right abstraction when you don't care about the exact host path. Bind mounts for development — mounting your source code into the container so code changes are reflected immediately without rebuilding. Also for injecting config files from the host. Never use in production if avoidable (host path dependency, platform-specific issues). tmpfs for secrets that must not hit disk (payment tokens, private keys during computation), caches that don't need persistence, or improving performance of write-heavy processes. The Permissions Gotcha "The most common bind mount pain point is file permissions. Your host user is UID 1000, the container user is UID 999 — suddenly you can't write to mounted files. Solutions: match UIDs, use ACLs, or use --user flag. In production, volumes sidestep this because Docker manages the path." Follow-ups → "How do you backup Docker volumes?" (docker run --volumes-from, or direct copy from /var/lib/docker/volumes) → "Volume drivers?" (NFS, AWS EBS, Azure File — for persistence that follows the container across nodes) 5. "How would you debug a container that's crashing on startup?" ▼ The Systematic Approach "I follow a consistent sequence: logs → exit code → interactive shell → image inspection." Step-by-step Step 1 — Logs : docker logs <container> (or --follow for streaming, --tail 100 for last 100 lines). 80% of crashes are diagnosed here — application error, missing env var, port conflict. Step 2 — Exit Code : docker inspect <container> --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}' . Exit 1 = application error. Exit 137 = OOMKilled (memory limit exceeded). Exit 139 = segfault. Exit 143 = SIGTERM received (graceful shutdown). Exit 125, 126, 127 = container runtime errors (bad CMD, permission denied). Step 3 — Override entrypoint : docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh -it <image> to get a shell and poke around. Check if files exist, env vars are set, the binary is executable. Step 4 — Inspect the image : docker inspect <image> to see configured CMD, ENTRYPOINT, ENV, working directory. docker history <image> to see all layers. Step 5 — Exec into running container : If the container runs briefly, docker exec -it <container> /bin/sh while it's alive. Or use a debug sidecar. Common Causes Missing environment variables (DB_HOST, API_KEY not set) Database not ready yet (startup race — use wait-for-it.sh or healthcheck-based depends_on) Port already in use on host Insufficient memory limits → OOMKilled Wrong architecture (ARM image on x86 or vice versa) File doesn't exist or isn't executable (wrong COPY path in Dockerfile) 6. "What Docker security practices do you follow in production?" ▼ Strong Opener "Container security is defense in depth. No single measure is sufficient. I think in four layers: image security, runtime security, host security, and network security." Image Security Pin base image versions with digest ( FROM node:18-alpine@sha256:... ), not just tags Run vulnerability scanners (Trivy, Docker Scout, Snyk) in CI — block on critical/high CVEs Use minimal base images: Alpine, distroless, scratch where possible — less software = less attack surface Multi-stage builds to exclude build tools from runtime images Never embed secrets in images (not in ENV, RUN, or COPY) Runtime Security --user nonroot or create a dedicated user in Dockerfile — avoid running as UID 0 --read-only root filesystem with explicit tmpfs mounts for writable directories --cap-drop ALL --cap-add <specific caps> — drop all capabilities, add only what's needed Custom seccomp profiles to restrict syscalls (Docker's default is already restrictive, but you can tighten further) --no-new-privileges — prevent privilege escalation via setuid binaries Production Story "We had a container escape near-miss where a misconfigured container had --privileged — someone had added it to debug a storage driver issue and it never got removed. We added an OPA policy to the admission controller that blocked privileged containers unless explicitly annotated with an approval. This kind of guardrail is essential at scale." 7. "If Kubernetes deprecated Docker, does that mean we can't use Docker images anymore?" ▼ Strong Opener "This is one of the most misunderstood announcements in the container world. Kubernetes deprecated dockershim — the compatibility shim that let Kubernetes talk to Docker's API. It did NOT deprecate Docker images. All Docker images follow the OCI image spec and work perfectly with containerd, CRI-O, and any other OCI-compliant runtime." Why it happened "Kubernetes communicates with container runtimes through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI). Docker's runtime didn't speak CRI natively, so Kubernetes maintained a translation layer (dockershim). This was extra complexity with no benefit — containerd (which Docker uses internally) does speak CRI. Removing dockershim meant Kubernetes could talk directly to containerd, skipping the Docker layer entirely." What actually changed Dev workflow: zero change — you still use docker build , docker push , Docker Desktop CI/CD: zero change — your pipeline still builds Docker images that Kubernetes pulls Cluster nodes: nodes no longer have Docker installed — they use containerd or CRI-O directly Debugging: you can no longer SSH into a K8s node and run docker ps to see pods (use crictl ps instead) The Insight That Impresses "This change actually exposed something important: Docker was always a developer experience layer on top of lower-level infrastructure. Containerd is the real runtime — Docker was always using it internally. The deprecation clarified the architecture: OCI images are the standard, and runtimes are interchangeable commodities." ← Learning Journey System Design → Section 04 · System Design System Design Integration Docker isn't just a deployment tool — it touches every pillar of system design. Understanding how containerization decisions ripple through reliability, cost, security, and observability is what separates architects from practitioners. How Docker Connects to System Design Pillars ⚡ Reliability Immutable images eliminate configuration drift. Health checks enable self-healing. But shared kernel means a kernel panic takes all containers on that host — VM-level blast radius for node failures. 📡 Availability Containers start in seconds enabling fast horizontal scaling. Zero-downtime deploys via rolling updates. But stateful containers are hard — databases need careful storage and connection management. 🏎️ Latency Container startup adds ~100ms overhead (vs ~1ms for a process). Container networking adds ~5-10μs per hop on bridge networks. DNS resolution in service meshes adds per-request overhead. Cold starts matter for serverless-style workloads. 🚀 Throughput Packing more containers per host (10-100x vs VMs) dramatically increases workload density. CPU and memory isolation via cgroups prevents noisy-neighbor problems that reduce effective throughput. 🔧 Maintainability Dockerfiles are infrastructure as code. Rolling back = redeploying a previous image tag. Immutable deployments mean no "snowflake servers." But Dockerfile complexity and base image maintenance add their own burden. 💰 Cost Higher server density reduces infrastructure cost. Faster build cycles reduce CI compute. But registry storage, egress for image pulls, and operational tooling add new cost lines often overlooked. 🔒 Security Process isolation improves over bare metal. Minimal images reduce attack surface. But container escape vulnerabilities, privileged containers, and the Docker socket as a root equivalent introduce new attack vectors. 📊 Observability Ephemeral containers make log collection critical — logs must be shipped before container dies. Container IDs constantly change — correlation requires labels, not hostnames. cgroups metrics enable per-container resource monitoring. System Design Scenario: CI/CD Pipeline with Docker Let's walk through how Docker fits into a complete CI/CD system design, and the decisions that matter. Docker in a CI/CD Pipeline — End to End Developer git push CI Runner docker build trivy scan run tests Registry ECR / Harbor myapp:abc1234 myapp:previous CD System docker pull rolling update health check Node 1 myapp:abc1234 Node 2 myapp:abc1234 Node 3 myapp:abc1234 Key System Design Decisions in This Pipeline Build Strategy Registry Design Deploy Strategy Rollback Plan Build Strategy Decisions Cache source : Where does the build cache come from? Local cache is fastest but CI runners are ephemeral. Registry-based cache (BuildKit --cache-from ) works across runners but adds ~30s for cache pull. S3-based cache is another option. Most teams settle on registry cache for balance. Build context size : Sending a large build context (huge node_modules, large assets) to the Docker daemon is a major CI bottleneck. A thorough .dockerignore is as important as Dockerfile optimization. Parallel builds : Multi-stage builds can run stages in parallel with BuildKit. For a monorepo building 20 services, build matrix in CI with registry cache reduces build time from 40min to 8min. Image tagging : Tag with git commit SHA (immutable + traceable) + branch name (mutable reference). Never use only latest in production — you lose the ability to audit what's deployed. Registry Architecture Decisions Public vs Private : Docker Hub for OSS projects and public base images. Private registry (ECR, GCR, Harbor) for proprietary applications — keeps images internal, avoids rate limits (Docker Hub: 100 pulls/6hr for anonymous, 200 for authenticated free accounts). Registry geography : If you deploy to multiple regions, push to regional registries to reduce pull latency. AWS ECR replication copies images across regions automatically. Cold pulls across continents can add 2-5 minutes to deployment time. Retention policy : Define when to delete old images — every untagged image consumes storage and costs money. Common policy: keep the last 10 tags per repo, keep images < 90 days, never delete tags matching semantic versioning patterns. Image scanning : ECR, GCR, and Harbor all offer integrated scanning. Shift scanning left: block CI if critical CVEs are found in the built image. Some teams also scan at pull time on K8s nodes. Deployment Strategy Rolling update : Replace containers one by one. Zero downtime if health checks are configured. Risk: brief period where old and new versions serve traffic simultaneously — backward-compatible API changes required. Blue-green : Maintain two identical production environments. Deploy to green, test, switch traffic. Immediate rollback by flipping back. Costs 2x infrastructure during transition. Best for risky releases. Canary : Route small percentage (1-5%) of traffic to new version. Monitor error rate, latency, business metrics. Gradually increase percentage. Requires traffic splitting (service mesh or weighted load balancer). Image pull policy : Always pull on deploy to get the latest security patches even if the tag hasn't changed? Or pull only when tag changes? IfNotPresent is faster but can miss security updates. Always is safer but slower and puts load on the registry. Rollback Strategy The Docker advantage : Rolling back is just redeploying the previous image tag. If you tagged with git commit SHA, you can deploy any commit's image instantly — no rebuilding needed. What rollbacks don't fix : Database schema migrations. If the new version ran a migration that removed a column, rolling back the app to the version that expects that column will break. This is why backward-compatible migrations (add column before deploying, remove column after old version is gone) are essential. Keep N previous images : Ensure your registry keeps at least the last 3-5 deployable images. If a critical bug shows up 2 hours later and you've already garbage-collected old images, you're rebuilding from source under pressure. Docker in Multi-Tier Architecture The Standard Three-Tier Containerized App Tier 1 — Load Balancer (nginx/HAProxy container) : Routes requests, terminates SSL. Typically 2 replicas for HA. Stateless — no persistent data needed. Tier 2 — Application containers : Stateless services. Scale horizontally. Multiple replicas behind load balancer. Health check on /health endpoint. No local state — session data in Redis. Tier 3 — Database (PostgreSQL/MySQL) : Stateful — requires persistent volume. Usually single primary in simple setups. Separate Docker network from app tier. Critical: resource limits set conservatively to avoid OOMKill during query spikes. When NOT to Containerize Docker Doesn't Solve Everything GPU workloads : Containerizing GPU-accelerated jobs requires NVIDIA Container Toolkit and careful driver management. Often simpler to use bare metal or dedicated GPU VMs. High-performance networking : Container network stack adds overhead. DPDK, RDMA, and SR-IOV applications may need host networking or bypass containers entirely. Legacy applications with kernel dependencies : Apps that depend on specific kernel modules, kernel version, or low-level OS features may not containerize cleanly. Very small teams, simple apps : A 3-person startup running a Rails monolith may find Docker and Kubernetes overhead higher than the benefit. Platform-as-a-Service (Heroku, Render) may be better. ← Interview Prep Ripple Effects → Section 05 · Ripple Effects Ripple Effects Map When an organization adopts Docker, the waves spread far beyond the ops team. The story of how we got here — and where we're going. 2013 — Year 0: The Demo Heard Round the Dev World Docker 0.1 Launches at PyCon Solomon Hykes' 5-minute demo: a Python application running in a container, built from a Dockerfile, and shipped as an image. The audience reaction was immediate — this solved a problem everyone had but couldn't articulate. State of the industry: Puppet, Chef, and Ansible were the state of the art for configuration management. Vagrant gave developers VMs. Heroku had pioneered 12-factor apps. AWS was dominant but deployments were still heavily manual. What Docker changed: It packaged the application AND its environment. Not "install our app on your environment" but "here is the environment, your app included." Technical foundation: Wrapped LXC (Linux Containers) with a simpler API and layered Union Filesystems. Introduced the concept of a Dockerfile as a reproducible build recipe. Open-sourced on GitHub immediately. 2014–2015 — The Cambrian Explosion Docker Inc. Raises $40M, Ecosystem Explodes Every major cloud provider and tool vendor announced Docker support within 18 months. Amazon Container Service, Google Container Engine, Microsoft Azure Containers all launched. Docker Hub went from 0 to millions of images. Docker abandons LXC: Docker 0.9 shipped libcontainer, a native Go library for container runtime, removing the LXC dependency. This was crucial for portability and gave Docker full control of the runtime. The orchestration problem emerges: Running one container is easy. Running 100 containers across 10 servers — deciding where each runs, restarting failures, networking them together — required new tooling. Docker Swarm, Google Kubernetes (June 2014), Mesosphere Marathon, and CoreOS Fleet all launched to compete. Fig becomes Docker Compose: Docker acquires Fig, the multi-container compose tool. Local development with multiple services becomes standardized. Security concerns emerge early: Docker's privileged mode, the Docker socket as root equivalent, and running containers as root-by-default drew scrutiny from security researchers. The NIST published early container security guidance. 2016–2017 — The Orchestration Wars Docker vs Kubernetes vs Mesos — and the Winner Emerges Three serious contenders: Docker Swarm (simplest, Docker-native), Kubernetes (backed by Google, most powerful), Apache Mesos with Marathon (best for mixed workloads, popular at Twitter/Airbnb). Companies placed bets. Kubernetes' secret weapon: It was based on Google's decade of experience running Borg — their internal cluster manager. Every design decision had been tested at billion-container scale. The design was complex but battle-proven. The CNCF formation (2016): Cloud Native Computing Foundation formed with Kubernetes as the first project. Google, IBM, Red Hat, and others donated massive engineering resources. Docker contributed containerd. Docker's strategic mistake: Docker Inc. tried to compete with Kubernetes rather than integrate it. The result: Kubernetes got all the enterprise attention. Docker eventually bundled Kubernetes in Docker Desktop but the perception had shifted. OCI standardization (2015-2017): The Open Container Initiative standardized image format and runtime spec. This was momentous: it decoupled the image format from any single vendor. Docker, rkt, Mesos could now run the same images. 2018–2019 — Kubernetes Wins, Runtime Decouples Containerd Graduates, BuildKit Arrives, Docker Inc. Struggles Kubernetes became the de-facto standard. Every major cloud offered managed Kubernetes. Docker Swarm adoption stalled. Docker Inc. laid off engineers and pivoted focus to developer tooling. containerd becomes independent: Docker donated containerd to CNCF. It became the reference container runtime for Kubernetes — the real runtime underneath, now independent of Docker. This was the beginning of Docker's decoupling from the runtime layer. BuildKit ships (Docker 18.09): A completely rebuilt build engine with parallel execution, improved caching, secret mounts, and SSH forwarding. Dramatically faster builds. Changed the Dockerfile development experience. Docker Desktop growth: Even as Docker Inc. struggled commercially, Docker Desktop became the dominant developer tool. VSCode's Remote Containers extension (2019) made developing-in-containers mainstream. The Mirantis acquisition (2019): Mirantis acquired Docker's Enterprise product line. Docker Inc. refocused on Docker Desktop and Docker Hub as developer tools. 2020–2022 — Kubernetes Removes Docker, Podman Rises Dockershim Deprecated — The "Docker is Dead" Non-Event Kubernetes 1.20 (December 2020) announced dockershim deprecation. The industry briefly panicked. Most infrastructure engineers realized: nothing in their workflow actually changed for end-users. What actually changed: Kubernetes nodes no longer ran Docker daemon. They ran containerd (or CRI-O) directly. You couldn't SSH into a node and run docker ps to see pods. You needed crictl instead. CI pipelines didn't change. Podman emerges seriously: Red Hat's daemonless, rootless container tool gained enterprise adoption. Podman is Docker-compatible (same CLI, same Dockerfiles) but doesn't require a running daemon. Better security story for servers. Docker Desktop licensing change (2022): Docker Desktop became paid for larger companies. This accelerated Podman, Lima, and Rancher Desktop adoption as alternatives on developer machines. Supply chain security spotlight: Log4Shell (December 2021) showed how transitive dependencies in container images could compromise thousands of services. SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation became a compliance requirement. Sigstore and cosign for image signing went mainstream. 2023–2025 — Maturity, Security, and New Frontiers BuildKit as Default, Docker Scout, and WASM Containers The container ecosystem reached maturity. The tools stopped changing quarterly and stabilized into supported, versioned products with clear support windows. Docker Scout (2023): Integrated vulnerability and software composition analysis. Developers see CVEs at build time in Docker Desktop. The shift-left security vision finally became practical. WASM containers (2023-2024): Docker announced WebAssembly container support. WASM modules can run as containers via the WasmEdge runtime, enabling near-native performance, language portability, and a security sandbox stronger than Linux namespaces. Still experimental but directionally important. AI/ML containerization: Every ML framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX) ships official Docker images. GPU-accelerated containers became standard. Large model serving (LLMs) drove requirements for specialized container runtimes with GPU passthrough. eBPF changes the game: Cilium (eBPF-based CNI) replaces iptables for Kubernetes networking, offering dramatically better performance and observability. Container networking is being reimplemented using eBPF programs loaded directly into the kernel. 2026–2028 — Where We're Heading Platform Engineering, Function-Scale Containers, AI-Assisted Dockerfiles Platform Engineering: Large organizations are building Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) that abstract Docker/Kubernetes entirely. Developers write code; the platform produces OCI images, deploys them, and manages the lifecycle. Backstage, Port.io, and similar tools define the developer interface. Function-granularity containers: Firecracker microVMs, WASM, and optimized cold-start runtimes are enabling container-per-request workloads. AWS Lambda runs your code in a microVM that starts in <100ms. The line between containers and functions is blurring. AI-generated Dockerfiles: LLMs generate surprisingly good Dockerfiles. The Dockerfile may eventually be an implementation detail — you describe your application, the platform produces the container artifact. The important knowledge becomes understanding what a good container looks like, not memorizing syntax. Confidential containers: Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP enabling encrypted containers where even the cloud provider can't read the workload memory. Critical for healthcare, finance, and AI model protection. ← Ripple Effects Patterns → Section 07 · Patterns Patterns & Anti-Patterns The difference between a good and bad container strategy is often not which tools you use, but how you use them. Here are the patterns that survive production — and the traps that look reasonable until they blow up. ✅ Proven Patterns 1. Multi-Stage Build Separate your build environment from your runtime environment Essential The pattern: Use multiple FROM statements in a Dockerfile. Stage 1 contains all build dependencies (compilers, test frameworks, dev libraries). Stage 2 starts fresh from a minimal base and only COPY the built artifact from Stage 1. Why it works: Build tools can be 10-100x larger than the actual application binary. A Go application binary is typically 10-20MB; the Go compiler toolchain is 800MB+. A React app's compiled output is 500KB; node_modules for building it is 300MB+. Real impact: Team at a fintech startup reduced their Docker image from 1.8GB to 47MB for a Node.js API. Deploy times fell from 8 minutes to under 90 seconds. The attack surface dropped by 97% (fewer installed packages = fewer vulnerabilities). When to use: Almost always for compiled languages (Go, Rust, Java, .NET). For interpreted languages (Python, Node), use it to separate build-time package installation from runtime, and to exclude test/dev dependencies. 2. Sidecar Container Pattern Extend a container's capabilities without modifying it Architecture The pattern: Run a secondary container alongside your main container that handles a cross-cutting concern: log shipping (Fluentbit), metrics collection (Prometheus exporter), configuration reload (Consul template), or network proxying (Envoy). Why it works: The sidecar handles infrastructure concerns so the application container stays focused on business logic. The application doesn't need to be modified to gain observability, security, or network capabilities. Classic example: Your legacy monolith can't push metrics in Prometheus format. Add a StatsD sidecar that accepts StatsD metrics and translates them to Prometheus. The monolith is unchanged. Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) use this pattern for every pod — inject Envoy sidecar, gain mutual TLS and traffic management for free. Docker Compose example: App container + Fluentbit sidecar. Both containers share a Docker volume where the app writes log files and Fluentbit reads and ships them to Elasticsearch. 3. Init Container Pattern Run setup tasks before your main container starts Architecture The pattern: Run a temporary initialization container before the main application container. The init container performs setup tasks — database migrations, schema validation, secret fetching, config generation — and must succeed before the main container starts. Why it works: Separates setup concerns from application concerns. The app container starts only when the environment is ready. Failed init = deployment stops before corrupting production state. In Docker Compose: Use depends_on with a health check — the migration container must exit 0 before the app starts. In Kubernetes, init containers are first-class: they run sequentially to completion before app containers start. Real example: Django application with PostgreSQL. Init container runs python manage.py migrate . If the migration fails (schema conflict, DB unreachable), the app never starts. No partial migrations in production. 4. One Process Per Container Containers should have a single, well-defined responsibility Principle The pattern: Each container runs exactly one process (or one cohesive process tree). Don't run nginx + application + cron + log shipper in a single container. Give each its own container. Why it works: Process isolation, independent scaling, independent failure/recovery, independent logging. If your web server crashes, it doesn't take down your cron jobs. You can scale web workers without scaling cron workers. The nuance: "One process" doesn't mean "one binary." A Node.js process with worker threads, or a Go binary with goroutines — that's fine. The principle is: one functional unit per container, not one OS process per container. 5. Immutable Infrastructure Never modify running containers — replace them Principle The pattern: To "update" an application, you don't exec into the container and change files. You build a new image, push it to the registry, and redeploy. The old container is replaced entirely. Why it works: Eliminates configuration drift (the "it worked differently in prod than in staging" problem). Every deployment is a clean slate from a known-good image. Rollback is just deploying the previous image. Audit trail is the image tag history. The corollary: No persistent data in containers. State must live in external volume
