Ecosystem Foundation & Context One Powerful Sentence Kubernetes is a platform for automating deployment, scaling, and operations of application containers across clusters of hosts. Not just "container orchestrator" — it's a data center operating system that treats entire fleets of servers as a single computer. Where Kubernetes Fits Developer Docker build Registry Docker Hub GCR / ECR Kubernetes Cluster Control Plane API Server Scheduler Controller Manager Node 1 Pod 1, Pod 2 Node 2 Pod 3, Pod 4 Node 3 Pod 5, Pod 6 External Traffic (Internet) Ingress → Service → Pod push deploy Kubernetes sits between your container registry and production infrastructure, managing deployment and scaling automatically. Why Kubernetes Exists The Problem: Container Sprawl In my 15 years, I've seen this pattern repeat: Companies adopt containers (Docker) because they solve the "works on my machine" problem. Then they hit a new wall: "How do we run 100 containers across 10 servers?" "What happens when a server fails?" "How do we update without downtime?" "How do we scale automatically?" The nightmare: You're now managing servers AND containers. Complexity exploded, not decreased. The Kubernetes Solution: Container Orchestration Kubernetes emerged from Google's 15+ years running containers at scale (Borg). It treats your entire data center as one big computer : Self-healing: Container crashes? K8s restarts it automatically Auto-scaling: Traffic spike? K8s adds more containers Load balancing: Distribute traffic across containers automatically Rolling updates: Deploy new versions without downtime Storage orchestration: Mount persistent volumes automatically The breakthrough: Declarative configuration. You tell K8s what you want , not how to do it . What Kubernetes is NOT ❌ Not a PaaS: You still need to understand Linux, networking, security ❌ Not magic: Complex distributed systems with new failure modes ❌ Not for everything: Simple apps? Overkill. Single server? Don't bother ❌ Not a complete solution: You need monitoring, logging, CI/CD around it Essential Abbreviations Decoded K8s K-eight-s Plain English: Abbreviation for "Kubernetes" (8 letters between K and s) Real-world: Like "internationalization" → "i18n" or "localization" → "l10n". It's just a shorthand because "Kubernetes" is long to type. Pod Pod Plain English: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — a group of one or more containers Real-world: Like a "pod" of whales — they travel together. Containers in a pod share the same network and storage, like roommates sharing an apartment. Node Node Plain English: A physical or virtual machine that runs pods Real-world: Like a worker in a factory. The node is the machine (worker), pods are the tasks assigned to it. Control Plane Control Plane Plain English: The "brain" of Kubernetes — makes global decisions about the cluster Real-world: Like air traffic control — doesn't fly planes itself, but directs everything, monitors the system, and responds to problems. YAML YAML (rhymes with camel) Plain English: The configuration language Kubernetes uses Real-world: Like a recipe card — tells Kubernetes exactly what you want (deployment with 3 replicas, expose port 8080, etc.). "YAML Ain't Markup Language" — it's for data, not documents. kubectl kube-cuttle" or "kube-control" Plain English: The command-line tool for controlling Kubernetes clusters Real-world: Like a remote control for your cluster. Every interaction with K8s happens through kubectl (or API calls under the hood). Service Service Plain English: A stable network endpoint that load balances traffic to pods Real-world: Like a phone number that forwards to multiple people. Pods (containers) come and go, but the Service IP/hostname stays the same. Ingress In-gress Plain English: Rules for routing external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to Services Real-world: Like a receptionist directing visitors to the right department. External traffic hits Ingress, which routes to Services based on URL paths. Historical Context: From Borg to Kubernetes Pre-2000 Google's Problem: Scale By early 2000s, Google was running thousands of services across massive clusters. Manual deployment was impossible. They needed automation. The pain: "We have the best engineers, but they're manually configuring servers instead of building products." 2003-2004 Borg is Born (Internal) Google built Borg — an internal container orchestration system. It ran billions of containers per week. The breakthrough: Treat the entire data center as one computer. Developers submit jobs, Borg decides where to run them. Key insight: Declarative API. Tell Borg what you want, let it figure out how. 2013 Docker Launches Docker makes containers accessible to everyone, not just Google. Suddenly, every company can use containers. The new problem: Companies adopt containers, then face the same orchestration challenges Google solved years ago. 2014 Kubernetes Launches Google open-sources Kubernetes (based on Borg lessons). Joe Beda, Brendan Burns, and Craig McLuckie lead the project. The vision: "Borg for the rest of us." Bring Google's operational expertise to the world. The community: Donated to CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation) in 2016. Neutral ground for collaboration. 2015-2017 Explosive Growth Adoption skyrocketed. Companies realized K8s solved real problems: 2015: v1.0 released. Production-ready. 2016: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud offer managed K8s. 2017: Docker Swarm vs Kubernetes war begins (K8s wins). 2018-2020 Kubernetes Wins By 2018, K8s is the standard. Even Docker embraces it. Major milestones: 2018: Docker Enterprise integrates K8s. 2019: K8s deprecates Docker as runtime (moves to CRI-O). 2020: CNCF survey: 83% of container users use K8s. 2021-Present Ecosystem Maturity Kubernetes is no longer a technology — it's infrastructure. Companies build on top: GitOps: ArgoCD, Flux for declarative deployments Service Mesh: Istio, Linkerd for service-to-service communication Serverless: Knative for serverless on K8s Edge: K3s, MicroK8s for edge computing The reality: K8s is the Linux of cloud — foundational infrastructure that everything else builds on. Core Concepts (The Mental Model) 🎯 Control Plane (The Brain) Makes global decisions: scheduling, responding to failures, scaling. Components: API Server, Scheduler, Controller Manager, etcd. 🧠 Like air traffic control — directs everything but doesn't fly planes 🖥️ Nodes (The Workers) Machines (physical or VM) that run containers. Each node has: kubelet (agent), kube-proxy (network), container runtime. 👷 Like factory workers — they do the actual work 📦 Pods (The Units) Smallest deployable unit. One or more containers that share storage/network. Always co-located, co-scheduled. 🐋 Pod of whales — travel together, same environment 🔄 Controllers (The Loopers) Reconciliation loops that watch desired state and drive actual state to match. Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet. 🔄 Thermostat — continuously checks temperature and adjusts Production Reality: What They Don't Tell You ⚠️ Kubernetes is Hard In my 15 years, I've seen companies adopt K8s and then: Spend months debugging networking: "Pod can't reach Service" becomes a full-time job Hit resource limits: "Why is OOMKilled my new best friend?" Face security nightmares: "Our control plane was exposed to the internet" Struggle with monitoring: "We have 1000 metrics but no idea what's happening" The lesson: K8s solves orchestration but introduces complexity. You need: monitoring, logging, security, GitOps, and expertise. ✅ When Kubernetes is Worth It Despite the complexity, K8s is absolutely worth it when: You're scaling beyond 10-20 servers: Manual management breaks down You need high availability: Self-healing prevents disasters You're doing multi-cloud: Same platform across providers You have complex microservices: Service mesh, traffic management, etc. Production reality: Every major tech company runs K8s at scale. It's the industry standard for a reason. 🎯 Key Takeaway Kubernetes exists because container orchestration at scale is incredibly hard . Google spent 15+ years figuring this out internally (Borg), then open-sourced the solution as Kubernetes. The core insight: Treat your entire data center as one computer. Declarative configuration (say what you want) + self-healing controllers (make it happen) = reliable infrastructure at scale. The trade-off: Kubernetes is complex and opinionated. But once it works, it works beautifully. You get reliability, scalability, and operational consistency that's impossible with manual management. What's Next 📊 Read the Analogy Understand Kubernetes through the "shipping port operations center" analogy. Next: Analogy → 🚀 Start the Journey Begin your 4-level learning path from beginner to expert. Start Journey → The Living Analogy 🏢 Kubernetes is Like a Shipping Port Operations Center Throughout this entire learning journey, we'll use the analogy of running a massive shipping port to understand Kubernetes. Everything you learn about Kubernetes will connect back to this analogy. The Core Analogy Kubernetes Concept Pod Smallest deployable unit - one or more containers Node Machine that runs pods Control Plane Brain that makes decisions Service Stable network endpoint for pods Deployment Manages replicated pods Ingress Routes external traffic Shipping Port Analogy 🚢 Shipping Container Standardized container that holds cargo (your application) 🏗️ Crane / Dock Worker Equipment/machines that move and process containers 🎯 Control Tower Operations center directing the entire port 📋 Shipping Manifest Document that identifies and routes containers 📦 Container Group Collection of containers traveling together 🚪 Port Gates Entry/exit point for external cargo/trucks Building on the Analogy Example 1: The "Pod" Concept 🚢 Shipping Container (Pod) In Kubernetes: A Pod is one or more containers that share storage/network. In the port: A shipping container holds cargo. Sometimes a container holds multiple items that travel together. Why this analogy works: • Containers are standardized (same size, same connectors) • They can be moved between ships (nodes) • What's inside varies (app, database, cache) • Multiple containers can be grouped (sidecar pattern) Production reality: Just as shipping containers revolutionized global trade by standardizing transport, Pods revolutionize deployment by standardizing application units. Example 2: Self-Healing and Auto-Scaling 🔄 Port Operations (Self-Healing) In Kubernetes: If a Pod crashes, K8s restarts it automatically. In the port: If a container falls off a crane, the operations center sees it and sends a replacement. The loop: 1. Control Tower: "Crane 3, what's your status?" 2. Crane 3: "Container fell. I have 9 instead of 10." 3. Control Tower: "Send replacement to Crane 3." 4. Crane 3: "Back to 10 containers." Production story: At a major company, we had a bug that caused crashes every 2 hours. With Kubernetes, no one noticed — it just restarted them. When we finally fixed it, we realized K8s had saved us from 2 months of outages. Example 3: Load Balancing ⚖️ Distributing Work (Load Balancing) In Kubernetes: Service distributes traffic across multiple Pods. In the port: Multiple cranes unload ships simultaneously. Trucks arrive and get directed to whichever crane has capacity. Without load balancing: Crane 1: 10 trucks waiting Crane 2: Idle, no trucks With load balancing (Service): • Trucks arrive at central office • Office directs: "Go to Crane 2" • Work distributes evenly • No one waits, no one sits idle The Service abstraction: Truck drivers don't need to know which crane to use. They just go to the "shipping office" (Service) and get directed. Example 4: Rolling Updates 🔄 Gradual Replacement (Rolling Updates) In Kubernetes: Update Pods one by one with zero downtime. In the port: Replace old containers with new ones without stopping operations. The rolling update process: 1. Bring new container to port 2. Stop ONE old container 3. Replace with new container 4. Verify it works 5. Repeat for next container Result: Port never stops operating. Ships keep getting unloaded. Production benefit: We deploy new code 100 times per day. With rolling updates, users never see downtime. They get new features gradually, and if something breaks, we rollback instantly. Example 5: The Control Plane 🎯 Operations Center (Control Plane) In Kubernetes: Control Plane makes global decisions and watches the system. In the port: The control tower sees everything and directs operations. What the Control Plane does: • API Server: Reception desk — receives all requests • Scheduler: Assigns containers to cranes (nodes) • Controller Manager: Ensures desired state (monitors and fixes) • etcd: Logbook — remembers everything The brain: It doesn't lift containers itself, but tells the cranes what to do. Key insight: The Control Plane is the intelligence layer. It knows the desired state ("We need 10 containers on each crane") and continuously drives reality to match. Example 6: Namespaces 🏢 Port Sections (Namespaces) In Kubernetes: Namespaces isolate resources within a cluster. In the port: Different sections for different companies or cargo types. Why namespaces matter: • Company A's containers go in Section A • Company B's containers go in Section B • They never mix, even though they share the port • Each has its own quota (resource limits) Benefit: Team A can't accidentally break Team B's deployment. Production reality: We run dev, staging, and prod in the same cluster but different namespaces. Saves money (shared infrastructure) while maintaining isolation. Example 7: ConfigMaps and Secrets 📋 Cargo Manifests (ConfigMaps/Secrets) In Kubernetes: ConfigMaps store configuration data; Secrets store sensitive data. In the port: Manifests that travel with containers explaining what's inside and how to handle it. ConfigMap (Cargo Manifest): • "This container contains electronics" • "Handle with care" • "Store in temperature-controlled area" Secret (Special Manifest): • "This container is valuable" • "Keep locked and secure" • "Only authorized handlers" Benefit: Configuration travels with the container, not hardcoded inside. Production best practice: Never put secrets in container images. Use Secrets (the locked manifest approach). This way, the same container can run in dev (test secrets) and prod (real secrets). Example 8: Persistent Volumes 🏭 Warehouses (Persistent Volumes) In Kubernetes: PersistentVolumes provide storage that survives pod restarts. In the port: Warehouses where goods are stored. Containers are temporary; warehouses are permanent. The storage problem: • Containers (Pods) are temporary — they come and go • But data needs to persist — databases, logs, uploads • Solution: Mount warehouse space to container PersistentVolume: "We have a warehouse with 100TB" PersistentVolumeClaim: "This container needs 10GB of warehouse space" Result: Container dies, data stays in warehouse Production story: We learned this the hard way. Deployed a database without persistent volume. Pod restarted → all data lost. Now: every stateful workload gets PV immediately. The Complete Mental Map 🚢 Shipping Port Operations Center The Kubernetes Analogy 🎯 Control Tower API Server = Reception Desk Scheduler = Assignment Manager Controller = Quality Control etcd = Logbook 🏗️ Cranes (Nodes) kubelet = Crane Operator kube-proxy = Traffic Director container runtime = Crane Mechanism 📦 Containers (Pods) Standardized units Can be grouped Moved between cranes Temporary but replaceable 📋 Operations Rolling Updates = Replace gradually Scaling = Add/remove cranes Healing = Fix broken containers Load Balancing = Distribute work 🔗 How We'll Reference This Analogy Throughout this learning journey, you'll see references to this shipping port analogy: When we talk about scheduling → Think "assigning containers to cranes" When we talk about services → Think "central shipping office" When we talk about volumes → Think "warehouse storage" When we talk about networking → Think "roads connecting cranes" When we talk about scaling → Think "adding more cranes or containers" When we talk about rolling updates → Think "replacing containers gradually" When we talk about namespaces → Think "sections of the port" 🎯 Why This Analogy Works The shipping port analogy captures Kubernetes' essence: coordinating massive numbers of standardized units (containers) through intelligent central control . Just as shipping ports revolutionized global trade by standardizing containers and automating their movement, Kubernetes revolutionizes deployment by standardizing application units and automating their orchestration. The key insight: You don't manually place every container. You declare what you want, and the operations center (Kubernetes) figures out how to make it happen. When in doubt, ask: "How would a shipping port handle this?" The answer usually points to the Kubernetes approach. Practice the Analogy Scenario 1: A Pod Crashes What happens in the port: A container falls off a crane during unloading. What the control tower does: Immediately notices on monitors. Alerts crane operator. Orders replacement container. Ensures the crane is back to full capacity. Kubernetes equivalent: Pod crashes → Kubelet detects → Controller Manager notices → Scheduler creates replacement Pod → Node runs new Pod → Service continues. Key insight: Human intervention not required. The system self-heals. Scenario 2: Traffic Spike What happens in the port: 100 trucks arrive when only 50 containers are being processed. What the control tower does: Sees backlog. Orders more containers brought from storage. Assigns more cranes to process them. Alerts all workers to increase throughput. Kubernetes equivalent: Traffic increases → HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) detects → Adds more Pods → Scheduler places them on Nodes → Service distributes traffic → System scales. Key insight: Scaling is automatic based on demand, not manual capacity planning. Scenario 3: New Software Version What happens in the port: New container design arrives. Need to replace all old containers gradually. What the control tower does: Brings new containers one at a time. For each crane, stops ONE old container, replaces with new, verifies it works, moves to next. Never stops operations. Kubernetes equivalent: Deployment update → Creates new ReplicaSet → Gradually scales up new Pods, scales down old Pods → Health checks → Rollback if issues → Zero downtime. Key insight: Updates happen gradually with continuous verification. If something breaks, rollback is instant. What's Next 🚀 Begin Your Journey Start the 4-level learning path from beginner to Kubernetes expert. Start Journey → 💬 Interview Prep Practice with interview-style conversation trees. Interview Prep → The Learning Journey: From Beginner to Expert Your path from "I've heard of Kubernetes" to "I can architect and operate production K8s clusters." This journey spans four levels, each building on the previous one with real-world experience and production insights. 1 Don't Break It 0-6 months 2 Comfortable Practitioner 6mo-2yr 3 Problem Solver 2-5yr 4 Architect's Mind 5-15+yr Level 1: The "Don't Break It" Stage Complete Beginner (0-6 months) Mental Model: The Shipping Port Dashboard At this level, think of Kubernetes as a control dashboard with buttons and displays. You don't need to understand the engine room — just which buttons to push and what the displays mean. kubectl apply → kubectl get pods → kubectl logs → kubectl delete The mantra: "I push these buttons in this order, and my app runs in the cluster." What Each Component Actually Does kubectl What it does: Your command-line interface to Kubernetes. Every interaction happens through kubectl (or API calls underneath). 🎛️ Analogy: Control panel at the shipping port operations center Pod What it does: The smallest deployable unit. One or more containers that share storage/network. Always co-located and co-scheduled. 📦 Analogy: Shipping container(s) that travel together Node What it does: A physical or virtual machine that runs pods. Each node has kubelet (agent), kube-proxy (network), and container runtime. 🏗️ Analogy: Crane/dock worker that moves containers Deployment What it does: Manages replicated pods. Ensures specified number of pods are running. Handles rolling updates and rollbacks. 📋 Analogy: Order: "Keep 10 containers of this type running at all times" Service What it does: Provides stable network endpoint (IP/DNS) for pods. Load balances traffic to pods. Pods come and go, Service stays the same. 📋 Analogy: Shipping office that directs trucks to available cranes Namespace What it does: Isolates resources within a cluster. Like virtual clusters within the physical cluster. 🏢 Analogy: Different sections of the port for different companies Safe Exploration Zones 🧪 Local Development Run K8s locally with minikube, kind, or Docker Desktop. Perfect for learning without breaking production. Run: minikube start to get a local cluster 📚 Read-Only Access Ask for read-only access to production clusters. You can look but not break. Use: kubectl get pods --namespace=production 🔧 Sandbox Namespaces Create your own namespace for experimentation. Can't affect others' resources. Create: kubectl create namespace my-sandbox Common Mistakes to Avoid (with Real Production Stories) ❌ "I'll run everything in the default namespace" MEDIUM SEVERITY The mistake: Deploying all apps to the `default` namespace. Everything mixed together. Real story: A new developer deployed their test app to default namespace, accidentally deleted what they thought was their pod, but it was someone else's critical service. Production outage for 2 hours. ✅ Right approach: Always use namespaces. Create one for your team, your app, your environment. kubectl create namespace myapp ❌ "I'll put secrets in my deployment YAML" CRITICAL SEVERITY The mistake: Adding database passwords and API keys directly in deployment manifests. Real story: A startup committed their deployment YAML to GitHub with AWS credentials in it. Within hours, their AWS bill was $50,000 from crypto mining. The credentials were in the repo for 6 months. ✅ Right approach: Use Kubernetes Secrets. Create secrets with kubectl create secret , reference in deployments. Never commit secrets to git. ❌ "I don't need resource limits" HIGH SEVERITY The mistake: Deploying pods without CPU/memory limits. One pod can hog the entire node. Real story: A data science job had a memory leak and consumed all node memory. The critical services running on that node (including monitoring) were OOMKilled. No one could see what was happening because monitoring died too. ✅ Right approach: Always set resources.requests and resources.limits. resources: {requests: {memory: "128Mi"}, limits: {memory: "256Mi"}} ❌ "I'll use latest tag for all images" HIGH SEVERITY The mistake: Deploying with image: myapp:latest . You have no idea what version is actually running. Real story: Team deployed with `:latest`. During incident, they couldn't roll back because they didn't know which version was previously deployed. Was it `latest` from today? Yesterday? Last week? ✅ Right approach: Use specific version tags. image: myapp:v1.2.3 . You can always update to newer versions, but you know exactly what's running. Basic Terminology with Analogies Cluster 🏢 Entire Port Collection of nodes (machines) running Kubernetes Control Plane 🎯 Control Tower Brain that makes decisions and coordinates the cluster etcd 📋 Logbook Key-value store that remembers the entire cluster state kubelet 👷 Crane Operator Agent on each node that runs pods and reports to control plane kube-proxy 🔀 Traffic Director Manages network rules on each node for Service communication Container Runtime ⚙️ Crane Mechanism Software that runs containers (containerd, CRI-O) Survival Checklist for Your First Week Install a local K8s: minikube start or kind create cluster Deploy your first app: kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx Expose it: kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80 --type=NodePort Check what's running: kubectl get pods and kubectl get all View logs: kubectl logs <pod-name> Get interactive: kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- sh Delete stuff: kubectl delete deployment nginx Understand the difference between kubectl apply and kubectl create Level 2: The "Comfortable Practitioner" 6 Months - 2 Years Mental Model: Understanding the System At this level, you move beyond "which buttons to push" to why things work the way they do . You understand Kubernetes' architecture and can troubleshoot issues. The shift: From "I run this command" to "I understand what this command is doing under the hood." Understanding Kubernetes' Architecture Kubernetes consists of two parts: Control Plane (the brain) and Worker Nodes (the muscle). Control Plane Components API Server: Front door for all operations. Authenticates, validates, configures data. etcd: Key-value store. The cluster's "memory" — remembers everything. Scheduler: Decides which nodes run which pods. Controller Manager: Runs controller loops. Notices desired vs actual state, drives to match. Worker Node Components kubelet: Primary node agent. Talks to API server, ensures pods are running. kube-proxy: Network proxy. Maintains network rules on each node. Container Runtime: Runs containers (containerd, CRI-O, etc.). Key insight: When you run kubectl apply , you're talking to the API Server. The API Server stores your desired state in etcd. Controllers notice the change and make it happen. The Scheduler decides where pods run. Kubelet on each node actually runs them. Why Features Exist (Design Principles) 🎯 Principle 1: Declarative API What it is: You tell Kubernetes what you want , not how to do it . Why it exists: Imperative approaches ("run container on node 3") don't scale. Declarative ("run 3 replicas, I don't care where") enables self-healing and automation. In practice: Imperative: "Run pod on node 3" → What if node 3 fails? What if you need to scale? Manual work. Declarative: "I want 3 replicas of nginx" → K8s figures out where, how to handle failures, auto-scales. 🎯 Principle 2: Controller Pattern What it is: Controllers continuously reconcile desired state (what you want) with actual state (what exists). Why it exists: Distributed systems are constantly changing. Nodes fail, pods crash, networks glitch. Controllers ensure the system self-heals. The loop: 1. Observe actual state (current pods: 2) 2. Compare with desired state (deployment wants: 3) 3. Take action to reconcile (start 1 new pod) 4. Repeat forever Production tip: This is why Kubernetes "just works" — controllers are constantly fixing problems. 🎯 Principle 3: Labels and Selectors What it is: Key-value pairs attached to objects. Selectors query for objects with specific labels. Why it exists: Enables loose coupling. Services don't know which pods they target — they query by labels. In practice: Pod has labels: app=nginx, tier=frontend Service selects: tier=frontend → Service finds all pods with that label, regardless of which pod they are Production story: We added a new pod version with labels app=nginx, version=v2 . Service selector app=nginx sent traffic to both v1 and v2. We tested v2, then removed v1 label. Zero downtime rollout. 🎯 Principle 4: Desired State and Reconciliation What it is: You declare desired state; K8s continuously drives actual state to match. Why it exists: Manual operations don't scale. Automation requires clear goals and autonomous correction. The reality: Kubernetes is not "set it and forget it" — it's "set it and it maintains itself". You still need to monitor, but much less manual intervention. Customizing Basics Confidently Writing Your Own Deployment Manifests Basic Deployment YAML Why: Declarative configuration, version controlled, reviewable, reproducible. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nginx-deployment labels: app: nginx spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: nginx template: metadata: labels: app: nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.21 ports: - containerPort: 80 resources: requests: memory: "128Mi" cpu: "100m" limits: memory: "256Mi" cpu: "200m" Breakdown: apiVersion (which API), kind (what type), metadata (name/labels), spec (what you want). The template is what each pod should look like. Service YAML Why: Stable network endpoint for your pods. Load balancing. apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nginx-service spec: selector: app: nginx ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 80 type: LoadBalancer Key concept: Selector matches pod labels. Port is what the service listens on. TargetPort is what pods expose. ConfigMap for Configuration Why: Separate configuration from code. Don't rebuild images for config changes. apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: app-config data: database_url: "postgres://localhost:5432/mydb" cache_enabled: "true" log_level: "info" Usage: Reference in deployment as environment variables or mounted as files. Secret for Sensitive Data Why: Store passwords, API keys, certificates separately. Base64 encoded (not encrypted by default, use external secret management). apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: app-secret type: Opaque data: password: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM= # base64 encoded Security note: Secrets are only base64 encoded. Use external secret management (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) for production encryption. Beginning Troubleshooting Methodology When Pods Won't Start 1 Check pod status kubectl get pods Look at STATUS column. Running? Pending? CrashLoopBackOff? ImagePullBackOff? Each means something different. 2 Describe the pod kubectl describe pod <pod-name> Shows events. This is your #1 debugging tool. Look for "Failed to pull image", "FailedScheduling", "OOMKilled". 3 Check the logs kubectl logs <pod-name> Shows what your application is logging. Container crashed? Logs will show why (often). 4 Get inside the pod kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- sh Interactive shell. See what's actually running. Check if files exist, network works, etc. 5 Check node resources kubectl top nodes Out of memory or CPU? Pods won't schedule. Nodes at capacity? Efficiency Basics and Patterns 📝 Use YAML, Not CLI Imperative commands ( kubectl run ) are fine for learning. Declarative YAML is required for production. Version control, review, rollback. kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml ← Do this kubectl run nginx --image=nginx ← Learning only 🏷️ Label Everything Labels make Kubernetes powerful. Query, group, select. Use consistent conventions: app=<name> , tier=<frontend/backend> , env=<dev/prod> . 📊 Set Resource Limits Always set requests and limits. Prevents noisy neighbor problems. Enables scheduling decisions. requests: minimum guaranteed (scheduling) limits: maximum allowed (throttling/eviction) 🔄 Use Liveness and Readiness Probes K8s needs to know if your pod is alive (restart if not) and ready (send traffic). Without probes, K8s can't self-heal properly. 🧹 Clean Up Old Resources Namespaces fill up with old deployments, jobs, pods. Regular cleanup: kubectl delete all --all in dev namespaces. 📚 Use Namespaces Organize by team, environment, project. Prevents accidental cross-team interference. Makes kubectl get pods manageable. Reading Between the Lines: What Documentation Means vs Says 📖 Documentation says: "Kubernetes is self-healing" Reality: Kubernetes self-heals if you configure it correctly. No probes? No resource limits? Bad YAML? It won't heal. Production lesson: Self-healing requires proper configuration: liveness/readiness probes, resource limits, replica sets, health checks. You get out what you put in. 📖 Documentation says: "Use Deployments for stateless workloads" Reality: Deployments work fine for many stateful workloads. But StatefulSets provide guarantees (stable network, persistent storage) that Deployments don't. Production lesson: Understand the trade-offs. Use the right tool. Deployments for most apps, StatefulSets for databases, queues, etc. 📖 Documentation says: "kubectl is the CLI for Kubernetes" Reality: kubectl is just an API client. Everything kubectl does, you can do with API calls. Many teams build custom tools on top of the API. Production lesson: Learn the API, not just kubectl. The API is the foundation. kubectl is just one interface. 📖 Documentation says: "Services provide load balancing" Reality: Services provide basic load balancing (random or round-robin). For advanced LB (session affinity, weighted routing), use Ingress or service mesh. Production lesson: Kubernetes LB is IPVS or iptables-based. Good for basics. Conversation 1: Kubernetes Fundamentals fundamentals architecture beginner-to-senior Q: "Explain Kubernetes architecture to me as if I'm a non-technical stakeholder." What they're testing: Can you simplify complex concepts? Do you understand the abstractions well enough to explain them without jargon? Talking Points Follow-up Questions Production Examples What If... 🎯 Core Talking Points (15+ years experience) Start with the business problem "Kubernetes solves the problem of running applications reliably at scale. Imagine you have 100 servers and 500 applications. Manually keeping everything running is impossible. Kubernetes automates this." Use the operations center analogy "Think of Kubernetes like a shipping port operations center. You have a control tower that sees everything, cranes that move containers, and automated systems that ensure the right containers are in the right place at the right time." Explain the what, not the how "You tell Kubernetes what you want: 'I need 10 copies of my web application running.' Kubernetes figures out how to make that happen, handles failures, and keeps 10 running no matter what." Self-healing is the key benefit "The magic is that Kubernetes is constantly watching. If a server fails, it moves applications to healthy ones. If traffic spikes, it automatically adds more capacity. It's like having an operations team that never sleeps." Business outcomes, not technical features "What this means for the business: We can deploy features faster (multiple times per day), handle more users without manual intervention, and recover from failures automatically. Our engineers spend time building features, not fixing infrastructure." 🔍 Follow-up Questions Based on Their Answer If they mention specific components (pods, services, deployments) "Great! What you're looking for: Mentions the control plane (scheduler, API server) Describes the reconciliation loop Understands rolling updates Can explain pod lifecycle If they stay too high-level "Let's dive deeper. How does Kubernetes actually know when to restart a failed pod? What's the mechanism?" What you're looking for: Kubelet watches pod status Controller manager reconciliation loops Desired state vs actual state If they seem nervous "It's okay to use technical terms. The solution: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with auto-scaling. The outcome: Scaled to over 1 million users in first week. Added clusters dynamically across regions. The New York Times The challenge: Modernizing legacy infrastructure. Moving from monolithic applications to microservices. The solution: Kubernetes on-premise for regulated workloads, GKE for others. The outcome: 50+ critical applications migrated. Improved deployment time from weeks to hours. Better resource utilization (40% cost savings). Key insight: "Kubernetes gave us flexibility. We can run workloads where it makes sense—on-prem or cloud—using the same platform." 🔄 "What If We Change..." Scenarios What if the candidate says "Kubernetes is just a container orchestrator"? The challenge: Push deeper. That's a beginner's answer. Your response: "That's true, but it's like saying 'a car is just an engine.' What does K8s actually do as an orchestrator? What problems does that solve that Docker alone doesn't?" Senior answer: "Kubernetes is a data center operating system. It treats entire fleets of servers as one computer, provides declarative configuration, self-healing controllers, and a uniform API for all infrastructure operations." What if they focus only on technical components? The challenge: They're missing the business value. Your response: "Great technical breakdown. Now imagine you're presenting to the CTO. Why did we invest millions in Kubernetes? What's the ROI?" Senior answer: "Kubernetes lets us ship faster, fail safely, and scale efficiently. Our deployment lead time dropped from weeks to minutes. Our MTTR (mean time to recovery) dropped from hours to seconds because pods auto-restart. We can handle Black Friday-scale traffic without pre-provisioning for months." What if they've never used the shipping port analogy? The challenge: Test if they can create analogies on the fly. Your response: "Good explanation. Now, create an analogy that a 12-year-old would understand. What is Kubernetes similar to in everyday life?" Strong answer examples: "Like a thermostat—you set the temperature, it maintains it automatically" "Like a warehouse manager who knows where everything is and moves things around as needed" "Like air traffic control—sees all planes, routes them to gates, handles delays" Conversation 2: Design Decisions & Trade-offs design trade-offs architecture Q: "Tell me about a time you had to make a difficult architectural decision with Kubernetes. What were the trade-offs?" What they're testing: Do they understand that every technical decision has trade-offs? Can they think critically? Do they learn from mistakes? 🎯 What You're Looking For (Senior Signs) They start with the business problem: Not "we used StatefulSets" but "we needed a database that could scale horizontally and survive node failures." They present options: "We considered three approaches: X, Y, and Z. Here's why we chose Y." They discuss trade-offs explicitly: "By choosing Kubernetes over ECS, we gained portability but lost simplicity. Our team needed more training." They admit mistakes: "In hindsight, we should have started with managed K8s instead of self-hosted. We spent 6 months learning what cloud providers already know." They discuss outcomes: "Six months later, here's what happened: our deployment frequency increased 10x, but our infrastructure complexity also increased." 🏭 Production War Story: Managed vs Self-Hosted K8s The situation: Mid-sized company (50 engineers) growing rapidly. Running microservices on ECS. Deciding whether to move to EKS (managed) or self-hosted K8s. The options: Option A (EKS - Managed): AWS manages control plane. $72/month per cluster. Limited customization. AWS lock-in. Option B (Self-hosted): Full control. No control plane cost. Complex operations. Build expertise or hire. Option C (GKE - Managed): Google's managed K8s. Better auto-scaling. Multi-cloud story. Team learning curve. The decision: Started with self-hosted K8s on EC2 to avoid vendor lock-in. What happened: Month 1-2: Team spent 80% time on K8s maintenance, not features Month 3: etcd corruption incident. Lost 4 hours trying to recover Month 4: Control plane upgrade failed. Cluster down for 2 hours Month 6: Realized: we're not a K8s vendor. We're building a product. The pivot: Migrated to EKS. Spent $72/month for control plane. Saved 100+ hours per month. The lesson: "Managed K8s isn't lock-in—it's buying expertise. AWS has 1000 engineers working on K8s. We have 2. Who do you think does it better?" The trade-off: We gave up some customization for reliability. But we can always run self-hosted clusters for special workloads. For 95% of apps, managed is the right choice. 🏭 Production War Story: Service Mesh Decision The situation: 50 microservices, growing communication complexity. Team debating: Istio, Linkerd, or no service mesh? The problem: Services can't reach each other consistently No observability into service-to-service calls Security: everything open, no mutual TLS Canary deployments require custom code The options analyzed: No mesh: Keep doing what we're doing. Simple but problems continue. Linkerd: Lightweight, Rust-based. Easy to install. Less feature-rich. Istio: Full-featured. Complex. Steep learning curve. More resources. The decision matrix: Team expertise: Low on service meshes. Need something learnable. Performance budget: Can't afford 50ms latency overhead. Complexity tolerance: Already running K8s, how much more complexity? Timeline: Need this working in 2 months, not 6. The choice: Started with Linkerd (v2). 15-minute install. Worked out of the box. Results after 6 months: Mutual TLS enabled everywhere automatically Can see 95th percentile latency per service Canary deployments reduced from custom code to YAML config Added 5-10ms latency overhead (acceptable) One engineer can manage it (part-time) The trade-off: Linkerd has fewer features than Istio (no advanced traffic shifting). But we don't need those features yet. When we do, we can migrate. The lesson: "Choose the simplest solution that solves your current problem. Don't build for theoretical future needs. Start simple, scale complexity as needed." 💬 Follow-up Discussion Questions "You mentioned trade-offs. What was the biggest downside of your decision?" Look for: Honest reflection. Not pretending everything was perfect. "If you could go back, would you make the same decision? Why or why not?" Look for: Growth mindset. What did they learn? "How did you convince stakeholders who disagreed with your approach?" Look for: Communication skills. Can they align teams? "What metrics did you track to know if the decision was successful?" Look for: Data-driven decisions. Not just gut feelings. "How would this decision be different if you had 10x the traffic? 1/10th the traffic?" Look for: Context awareness. One size doesn't fit all. Conversation 3: Performance & Scaling at Scale performance scaling production Q: "We're hitting Kubernetes performance limits. What do you do?" What they're testing: Have they actually run K8s at scale? Do they know where bottlenecks occur? Can they debug performance issues systematically? Systematic Approach Common Bottlenecks Real Incidents Prevention 🔍 Systematic Debugging Approach (15+ years experience) 1 Define "Performance Limits" Ask: What's actually slow? Pods not scheduling? API server timeouts? High latency? Nodes at 100% CPU? Senior insight: "Performance" means different things. First, measure. Establish baseline. Identify symptoms before treating. 2 Measure Everything Metrics to collect: Control plane: API server latency, etcd requests, controller queue depth Nodes: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network bandwidth Kubelet: Pod startup time, container runtime operations Network: Packet loss, latency between components Tools: Prometheus + Grafana, Kubernetes metrics API, node exporter 3 Identify the Bottleneck Common patterns: API server overwhelmed → Too many watches, large list operations etcd slow → Large cluster state, too many objects Scheduler backlog → Unschedulable pods, complex constraints Node pressure → Resource exhaustion, kubelet issues Senior insight: The bottleneck is rarely where you think. Measure, don't guess. 4 Address the Root Cause Not symptoms: Don't just add nodes. Fix the underlying issue. Examples: Too many watches → Reduce informer cache, optimize controllers Large etcd → Event TTL, compact etcd, reduce object count Scheduler slow → Tune scheduler profile, remove complex affinities Network issues → Check MTU, DNS, CNI configuration 5 Verify & Monitor After fix: Did it improve? Side effects? New problems? Long term: Set up alerts. Next time, catch it early. Senior insight: Every fix has trade-offs. Monitor for unintended consequences. 🚧 Common Performance Bottlenecks API Server Overload Symptoms: kubectl commands timeout Controllers can't watch resources Webhooks fail with connection errors Causes: Too many clients watching resources (hundreds of controllers) Large list operations (kubectl get pods --all-namespaces on 10k+ pods) Expensive admission webhooks (validation blocks requests) High churn rate (constantly creating/deleting resources) Solutions: Increase API server replicas and add load balancer Enable client-side throttling in controllers Optimize webhooks (async validation, caching) Use --request-timeout to prevent backlog etcd tuning: increase quota, compact more frequently Production story: A company had 50 microservices, each with a custom controller. All controllers watched Deployments. API server CPU hit 100%. Fixed by implementing informer caches with shared watches. Reduced API server load by 80%. etcd Performance Symptoms: API server shows "etcd request timeout" Cluster state changes take seconds to propagate etcd high CPU or I/O Causes: Too many objects (10k+ pods, 100k+ total resources) Large objects (massive ConfigMaps, Secrets) No compaction (etcd database grows unbounded) Network latency between API server and etcd Solutions: Enable --quota-backend-bytes (increase from 2GB default) Compact etcd hourly (auto-compaction) Enable event rate limiting and TTL Split etcd: events vs main data Move etcd to fast SSDs, separate disk Monitor etcd request latency (should be < 50ms p99) Production story: Company had 15,000 pods in one cluster. etcd database grew to 8GB. API server timeouts on every deploy. Fixed by: (1) Auto-compact etcd every hour, (2) Event TTL of 1 hour, (3) Separate etcd for events. Database size stabilized at 2GB. Scheduler Backlog Symptoms: Pods stuck in Pending state kubectl describe pod shows "FailedScheduling" Logs show "scheduler took too long" Causes: Complex scheduling constraints (affinity, anti-affinity, taints) Not enough resources (cluster at capacity) Too many unschedulable pods clogging the queue Scheduler evaluating thousands of nodes Solutions: Scale scheduler replicas (default 1, increase to 2-3) Simplify scheduling constraints (use defaults) Add nodes or remove resource limits Enable scheduler profiling to find slow operations Use pod priority and preemption for critical pods Consider multiple schedulers for different workloads Production story: Data science team submitted 5,000 ML training jobs at once. All pods had complex GPU affinity rules. Scheduler couldn't keep up. Fixed by: (1) Batch pod submission, (2) Simplified affinity rules, (3) Separate scheduler for batch jobs. Node Issues Symptoms: High CPU steal time Pods frequently OOMKilled Disk pressure, pods can't start Causes: No resource limits → noisy neighbor problem Over-provisioning (100% CPU requested on all nodes) Small nodes (too many pods per node) Slow container runtime (Docker vs containerd) Solutions: Always set requests and limits Monitor actual usage, adjust based on real data Use larger nodes with fewer pods (e.g., 64 pods vs 110 default) Switch from Docker to containerd or CRI-O (faster) Enable CPU QoS (Guaranteed > Burstable > BestEffort) Production story: Cluster had 500 small nodes. CPU overhead from K8s components was 30%. Consolidated to 100 large nodes. Overhead dropped to 10%. Same capacity, less complexity, lower cost. 🚨 Real Performance Incidents CRITICAL API Server DoS by Misconfigured Controller The setup: Company built custom operator to sync secrets from external vault to K8s. The bug: Operator had bug where it called API server every 100ms to list secrets. The impact: API server CPU hit 100% All deployments blocked (couldn't create new pods) Existing controllers couldn't watch resources (backlog overflow) Cluster frozen for 45 minutes The fix: Identified operator via API server audit logs (one client with 90% requests) Deleted operator deployment API server recovered within 2 minutes Fixed operator to use informer cache instead of polling The lesson: "Bad code can take down the entire cluster. Always rate-limit clients. Use watch/informer patterns, not polling." Prevention: Enable API server priority and fairness Monitor per-client request rates Set up alerts for API server CPU > 70% HIGH Large ConfigMap Causes etcd Timeout The setup: Team stored 50MB JSON config in ConfigMap. The problem: ConfigMap was mounted as volume in 500 pods. The impact: Every pod update triggered ConfigMap watch update API server tried to send 50MB payload to 500 clients etcd timeout on write operations Updates taking 30+ seconds The fix: Moved config to external object storage (S3) ConfigMap now contains S3 URL (< 100 bytes) Application fetches config from S3 on startup The lesson: "K8s stores are for metadata, not data. Large objects break etcd. Use external storage for anything > 1MB." Guideline: ConfigMaps should be < 1MB. Secrets < 1MB. If larger, use external store + reference. MEDIUM Event Storm Causes API Server Slowdown The setup: Application with bug that crash-looped every 2 seconds. The problem: Each crash created a Kubernetes event (warning message). The impact: 30 events per second = 2,600 per hour = 62,000 per day Events stored in etcd etcd grew from 2GB to 6GB in one week API server slower as etcd grew The fix: Fixed crash-looping application Deleted old events: kubectl delete events --all --all-namespaces Configured event TTL (1 hour) The lesson: "Events consume resources. Set TTL. Delete old events regularly. Don't let them accumulate." Prevention: Set --event-ttl in kube-apiserver (default 0 = no expiry). Use 1h or 24h. 🛡️ Prevention Strategies 1. Set Up Performance Baselines Before problems occur: Measure normal API server latency (should be < 100ms p99) Track etcd request latency (< 50ms p99) Monitor scheduler queue depth (should be near 0) Record node resource usage patterns Tooling: Prometheus + Grafana dashboards. Alert on anomalies (2x baseline). 2. Resource Limits for Everything Ensure every pod has: CPU requests (guaranteed minimum) CPU limits (max allowed) Memory requests (guaranteed minimum) Memory limits (max allowed, triggers OOM) Why: Prevents noisy neighbor. Scheduler can make good decisions. No surprise OOMs. Enforcement: Admission webhook that rejects pods without resource limits. 3. Right-Size Your Cluster Avoid these common mistakes: Too many small nodes: High overhead from system components. Aim for fewer, larger nodes. Over-provisioned: 80% of requested capacity unused. Wastes money. Under-provisioned: No room for failover. One node failure cascades. Guideline: Keep cluster at 70% capacity (30% headroom for spikes/failures). Use Cluster Autoscaler. 4. Separate Control Plane and Workload Best practice: Dedicated nodes for control plane components (etcd, API server, scheduler). Why: Control plane needs consistent resources. Workload spikes shouldn't affect K8s components. Implementation: Taint control plane nodes. Only system pods can schedule there. 5. Monitor Client Behavior Track per-client metrics: Request rate per client (QPS) Which resources they watch Request latency per client Why: Identify bad actors before they take down the cluster. Action: Throttle or block misbehaving clients automatically. 6. Limit Object Counts Set quotas: Max pods per namespace Max services per namespace Max ConfigMaps/Secrets Why: Prevents accidental or malicious resource explosions. Tool: ResourceQuota objects. Conversation 4: Failures & War Stories debugging failures real-world Q: "Tell me about a Kubernetes failure you experienced. How did you debug it? What did you learn?" What they're testing: Do they have real production experience? Can they debug systematically? Do they learn from failures? 🏭 War Story #1: The Silent Pod Killer (OOMKilled Mystery) Symptoms Application pods randomly disappearing. No logs. No errors. Just... gone. kubectl get pods showed: STATUS = OOMKilled. Restart count increasing. Investigation Step 1: Checked pod logs. Nothing helpful. Application didn't log anything before death. Step 2: kubectl describe pod. Found: Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 Step 3: Checked pod resource limits. Found: memory request: 256Mi memory limit: 512Mi Step 4: Question: Was application actually using > 512Mi? Step 5: Enabled memory monitoring. Found: Java app (Spring Boot) Heap size: Not set (default = 1/4 container memory = 128Mi) Non-heap memory: Native code, stacks, thread overhead Total RSS: 480-510Mi (hovering at limit!) Spike during GC: 550Mi → BOOM Root Cause Java application + Kubernetes = memory confusion. K8s limit: 512Mi (process container can't exceed this) JVM heap: 128Mi (default) JVM non-heap: 350Mi (native code, metaspace, stacks) Total: 478Mi normal, 550Mi spike The application wasn't configured for containers. JVM didn't know it was in a 512Mi limit. The Fix Immediate: Increased memory limit to 1Gi. Pods stopped dying. Proper fix: Configure JVM for containers: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 (use 75% of container memory) Now heap = 384Mi (75% of 512Mi) Non-heap = 128Mi Total = 512Mi (safe!) Lessons Learned Memory limits != application memory usage. Include overhead (runtime, stacks, native code). Monitor actual usage. Don't guess. Use Prometheus, cAdvisor. Configure runtimes for containers. JVM, Go, Node.js all have memory tuning. OOMKilled is silent. App can't log when OOM kills it. Monitor from outside. Test limits. Load test to find real memory usage, not just "it seems to work". Interview Follow-ups to Ask "How would you prevent this in the future?" → Admission webhook requiring memory limits for all Java apps. "What if you couldn't increase the memory limit?" → Optimize application, reduce heap, run multiple smaller pods. "How would you alert on this?" → Monitor OOMKilled events, alert if restart rate > threshold. 🏭 War Story #2: The DNS Resolution Disaster Symptoms Intermittent network failures. Service A can't reach Service B. Works 95% of the time, fails 5%. Errors: "dial tcp: lookup service-b.default.svc.cluster.local: no such host" Investigation Step 1: Checked Service B. Existed. Endpoints correct. Step 2: Checked DNS. CoreDNS pods running. No restarts. Step 3: Exec into pod, run nslookup: nslookup service-b.default.svc.cluster.local Sometimes worked, sometimes timed out. Step 4: Checked CoreDNS logs. Found: [INFO] 10.244.1.5:12345 - 12345 "A IN service-b.default.svc.cluster.local. default udp 512" SERVFAIL 2 High rate of SERVFAIL errors. Step 5: Checked CoreDNS metrics: DNS request rate: 50,000 QPS CoreDNS pods: 2 CPU per pod: 80-90% Latency: P99 = 2 seconds (should be < 50ms) Root Cause Cluster was too big for 2 CoreDNS pods. 5,000 pods Each pod makes DNS queries: other services, external APIs, etc. 50,000 QPS total DNS traffic 2 CoreDNS pods → 25,000 QPS each → CPU saturated When CPU at 100%, CoreDNS drops requests → SERVAIL Added to problem: Node local DNS cache not enabled. Every DNS query hit CoreDNS. The Fix Immediate: Scale CoreDNS to 10 replicas. Now 5,000 QPS per replica → CPU dropped to 20% Latency: P99 = 30ms SERVFAIL errors disappeared Long-term: Enable NodeLocal DNSCache. DaemonSet runs DNS cache on each node Pods query local cache (instant, no network hop) Cache misses go to CoreDNS Reduced CoreDNS load by 90% Lessons Learned DNS is critical infrastructure. When DNS fails, everything fails. Scale CoreDNS with cluster size. 2 replicas is too small for production clusters. Monitor DNS latency and error rate. Alert before it breaks. Enable NodeLocal DNSCache. Dramatically improves DNS performance and reliability. The "it works mostly" trap. 5% failure rate is unacceptable. Debug intermittent issues immediately. 🏭 War Story #3: The Rolling Update Rollback Symptoms Deployed new version. Rolling update started. 10% of pods updated. Then... nothing. Pods stuck at 10%. New pods crash-looping. Old pods still serving traffic. Deployment frozen. Can't move forward. Can't roll back automatically. Investigation Step 1: kubectl get pods. Saw: 5 old pods: Running 5 new pods: CrashLoopBackOff 5 pending: Not scheduled yet Step 2: kubectl logs new-pod-xyz. Error: Error: Database connection failed. Invalid password. Step 3: Checked ConfigMap/Secret. Found problem: New version uses different database (PostgreSQL vs MySQL) Deployment manifest had Secret reference Secret exists... in dev namespace Deploying to prod
